11147-phebe-the-blackberry-girl:
Uncle Thomas's Stories for Good Children includes this 1850 tale, Phebe, the Blackberry Girl, published at Worcester by Edward Livermore. The series aims to give young children information joined with amusement, and, if they acquire a love for good books, the compiler's object is accomplished. Contents add Good Children, Poor Crazy Robert, The Pet Lamb, Father William and the Young Man, and Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.

Phebe climbs a fence on the nearest way to town, catches her apron on a stake, tumbles down, scratches her arm, and scatters her blackberries in sand and dirt. A pretty little miss stops, pities her, and learns Phebe's father is very poor, works in a stall, and cannot clothe all his little ones. The verse tale teaches sympathy for poor children and gratitude for small kindnesses.
12086-eastern-shame-girl:
Translated from the French of George Soulie de Morant and privately printed in New York in 1929, this volume renders Chinese tales from seventeenth-century classical sources. Morant worked from Ming stories, and the book later appeared as Chinese Love Tales, winning a court fight over its literary merit.

Six tales follow students, singing girls, wives, and monks through love, betrayal, and revenge. A scholar falls for a famous courtesan; a wife error with an embroidered slipper sets off ruin; a monastery hides a complicated marriage. Erotic scenes sit beside moral judgments, and ghosts and fate press on the living. The book offers Western readers of its day a rare, if filtered, window onto late imperial Chinese storytelling.
12357-the-case-and-the-girl:
Randall Parrish published The Case and the Girl in 1922, a detective romance. Parrish, a prolific writer of mysteries and westerns, builds the plot around a young lawyer named West and a lady in a limousine.

Chapters run from a sudden engagement and the Coolidge home through untangling threads. Later come a visit to the indigent, an unexpected dismissal, the body of a suicide, suspicion verified, and a stone wall. A mid-book fight has West strike a red-haired man again and again, driving him prone before others drag him away. The case turns on identity, money, and a choice West must make facing death. The novel mixes courtship with detection in Parrish brisk manner.
12858-the-lilac-girl:
Ralph Henry Barbour's 1909 novel The Lilac Girl opens at a campfire in Saddle Pass, in the Sangre de Cristo Range of southern Colorado. Two men sit out a chill June evening in the mountains. The story soon turns to Wade, a young man, a house that may or may not be his, and a girl glimpsed over lilac sprays. Illustrations by Clarence Underwood mark key scenes.

A mid-book scene finds Wade relieved to find himself in his own house, sinking into a green rocker while Zephania sings upstairs about a wandering sheep. Barbour mixes western setting with gentle romance and mistaken identity. The novel offers light, pleasant reading in the author's popular vein.
13324-apples-ripe-and-rosy-sir-and-other:
Mary Catherine Crawley offers a set of short moral tales for boys and girls, reprinted from the Ave Maria and published in 1893. Children build boats, hang May baskets, give May-day gifts, and learn the price of greed in stories such as A Miser's Gold and That Red Silk Frock.

The title story opens in a hard March, and later tales follow first communicants home from Mass, a lesson with a sequel, and Uncle Tom's story. Kindness, honesty, and fair dealing win out over show and selfish gain. Written for young Catholic readers, the book keeps its lessons inside lively scenes of home, school, and parish life.
14087-the-jungle-girl:
Gordon Casserly's 1922 novel of British India opens with pigsticking, the boar hunt that tests a young officer's nerve. Frank Wargrave, posted near the Terai jungle, meets soldiers, planters, and a forest girl whose life sits outside cantonment rules. Elephants, trophies, and hill bungalows fill the background. A tiger country of heat, dust, and sudden rain sets the mood.

Love and duty pull Wargrave in opposite directions. A border outpost, a sentence of exile, and a strange rescue force him to weigh orders against feeling. Casserly knew the army life he describes, and the chapters on sport, mess talk, and jungle travel read as lived detail. Romance carries the plot, but the book's lasting pull is its picture of India at the edge of empire, where British routine meets a wilder world.
14169-ethel-hollister-s-second-summer-as:
Irene Elliott Benson's 1912 girls' book sends Ethel Hollister back to camp for a second summer, after a first book launched by her great-aunt Susan of Akron. Ethel plans, enters college, and grows firm friends with Harvey. Camp chapters bring Uncle John, a mother's visit, scouts arriving, and Nora giving service. A heroine emerges, camp breaks up with a surprise, and Mattie makes good.

Home life fills the second half. Judge Sands and Kate marry, a birthday present arrives, and Christmas Eve and Day bring fresh surprises. Mr. Casey buys a house, and Archibald changes for the better. One tender scene finds a judge asking his daughter Patty about a stepmother, until she guesses Kate Hollister with joy. Clean, cheerful, and earnest about service, the book shows Camp Fire ideals in action: work, friendship, and kindness practiced outdoors.
14598-the-goose-girl:
Harold MacGrath's 1909 romance, illustrated by André Castaigne, follows a goose girl acclaimed as queen in a Ruritanian kingdom of kings, chancellors, and vintners. Bobbs-Merrill published it in Indianapolis.

Gretchen, an American, and a young vintner move through affairs of state, socialists, love's doubts, twin lockets, and a white scar. Carmichael waits in a chancellor's cabinet with Grumbach and a police officer, and MacGrath's stage experience shows in the dialogue. MacGrath writes with theatrical flair. The novel is a light, romantic adventure in the Graustark manner, full of disguise and court intrigue.
15014-winnie-childs-the-shop-girl:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson's 1916 novel follows Winnie Childs, a young woman who works behind a shop counter and dreams of a wider life. The story opens at sea, where a chance meeting with Peter Rolls sets off a chain of mix-ups, secrets, and new chances. Its pace is quick, and its mood is warm and romantic.

Winnie moves between work, friendship, and love, testing her nerve as she faces rivals, family claims, and her own past. Peter, kind but restless, proves a steady foil to her pluck. Readers who enjoy old-fashioned romance with a plucky heroine and a happy-ending drive will find the book easy, lively company.
15714-the-poor-little-rich-girl:
A 1912 novel by Eleanor Gates, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York. Gwendolyn, a rich little girl, lives in a grand house where servants, not parents, rule her days. Gates, who wrote the tale for the stage as well, makes wealth itself the villain. The opening finds Gwendolyn staring at a tiny ink line on a gilt mirror, pale with a child's fear.

Gwendolyn longs for both father and mother in the nursery at once, a rare event in her managed life. Nurses, tutors, and rules fence her in, while poor children outside seem free. Her small rebellions and sorrows build to a plea for love over luxury. The novel endures as a sentimental classic: a child with everything except the one thing money cannot buy.
1612-poems-by-a-little-girl:
Hilda Conkling's Poems by a Little Girl, with a preface by Amy Lowell, gathers verses written by a child, for her mother and for the world. Dreams for her mother, like a soft thick fringe to hide her eyes, surprises shaped like strange butterflies, and songs twisted into poems fill a small, remarkable book.

Conkling, still a girl, writes with a fresh, musical imagination, of nature, home, and wonder, without adult polish. Lowell's preface presents her as a genuine child poet. The book is a charming curiosity, and a moving record of a young mind at play with words.
16514-a-little-cook-book-for-a-little-gi:
Caroline French Benton wrote this 1905 cook book for young girls, most of it first printed in Good Housekeeping. It opens with what Margaret made for breakfast, then teaches cereals step by step: a quart of boiling water, salt, and careful overnight cooking in a double boiler. Later recipes follow the same plain, patient method.

Benton dedicates the book to three little girls who love little-girl cooking. The tone is kind and practical, treating a child cook as a real cook. For readers of domestic history, it shows how Edwardian girls learned kitchen skills, one simple dish at a time.
1733-the-red-cross-girl:
Richard Harding Davis gathers stories around the Red Cross girl of the title, a young woman who serves in wartime and whose courage unsettles the men around her. Other tales in the volume take up the Grand Cross of the Crescent, an invasion of England, and a sailorman. An introduction by Gouverneur Morris sets Davis in his time.

The stories show Davis the correspondent turning reporter into romancer: hospitals, camps, and ships drawn from what he had seen, with heroines given the same nerve as his heroes. It is a wartime collection of its period, and its title story remains the best entry point, brisk, sentimental, and fond of a brave girl.
17418-the-black-pearl:
Mrs. Wilson Woodrow's 1912 Black Pearl opens at sunset, as a train crawls across the desert to Paloma, not many miles from the Salton Sea. One lone passenger descends: Rudolf Hanson, brought by curiosity or business to a station of little importance. Beyond the village, green foothills and pine-shadowed slopes rise like an oasis from artesian wells.

From that desert arrival grows a novel of California's Salton country, its people, and its secrets, told in Woodrow's colorful, popular prose. Illustrations mark the heroine's stand, the black pearl alone, and a branch bent over a fallen man. Readers who like western romance will enjoy a vivid, old-style tale of a desert town and its hidden treasure.
18505-a-popular-schoolgirl:
Angela Brazil wrote this school story, published in New York by Frederick A. Stokes in 1920, with pictures by Balliol Salmon, and first published in the United States in 1921. A Popular Schoolgirl follows Ingred and her schoolmates through a school year at Wynch-on-the-Wold. The book opens at the end of the holidays, with a boyish voice shouting for Ingred as its owner jumps a gooseberry bush and tears round the house.

Chapters give opening day, intruder Bess, the fifth-form fete, the school parliament, hockey, an unpleasant experience, a hostel frolic, and the whispering stones. Later chapters bring a strike, the rainbow league, Quenrede coming out, a peep-hole, an Easter pilgrimage, rivals, and the abbey recital. Girls get a classic Brazil school tale: friendship, rivalry, games, and the small politics of a girls' school, told with high spirits.
18666-polly-a-new-fashioned-girl:
L. T. Meade published this girls' novel at New York in 1910. Its heroine, Polly, faces a great misfortune on a hot July day, and the first part follows her family schemes, raids, attic games, and run-ins with Aunt Maria and Dr. Maybright. Chapters with titles such as Indigestion Week, A Was an Apple Pie, and Where Are the Children set a playful, bustling tone.

The second part brings new faces, a young Australian, a hermit's hut, rough weather, and a rescue, closing one year after. Meade, a veteran writer of girls' tales, keeps Polly bold and kind through scrapes and lessons. The novel is a lively period piece for young readers.
1867-the-diary-of-a-goose-girl:
Kate Douglas Wiggin's Diary of a Goose Girl, illustrated by Claude A. Shepperson, follows a young woman who takes charge of a flock of geese and keeps a diary of their doings. The geese, with a mother who accepts twelve orphans cheerfully, stretch their wings and look on the world with round, kind eyes.

Wiggin writes the diary with humor and tenderness, and the book's charm lies in its small scale: a girl, a farm, and birds who become individuals. Readers who love Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm will recognize the same warmth. The diary remains a light, sunny piece of farm writing for children and grown readers alike.
19310-happy-pollyooly-the-rich-little-po:
Edgar Jepson wrote this 1915 children's novel, Happy Pollyooly, the rich little poor girl. Reginald Birch drew its pictures. The Honourable John Ruffin makes an arrangement, and Hilary Vance finds a confidante. Infuriated swains appear, a duchess has an idea, and Pollyooly is called in. She plays her favourite part. The front piece shows her biting the end of her pencil.

Ruffin, bound for Buda-Pesth, asks Vance to house Pollyooly and the Lump. They would take his spare room. He promises grilled bacon worth learning about. Vance admits he does not like bacon, yet finds Pollyooly a delight to the eye. Readers get a light, witty Edwardian tale of a clever poor girl among rich folk.
19539-the-stowaway-girl:
Louis Tracy wrote this sea adventure novel; its New York printing appeared in the early nineteen hundreds with pictures by Nesbit Benson. The ship Andromeda sails, nears her voyage's end, and meets disaster, leaving refugees to face the sea between a Brazilian devil and the deep Atlantic.

A stowaway girl at the heart of the tale must win protection and trust among strangers, while pursuits and meetings on the high seas drive the plot. Tracy's brisk chapters keep the action moving from ship to shore and back again. After the wreck, chapters titled Cross Purposes and The Rigor of the Game carry the survivors' quarrels ashore.
20106-how-ethel-hollister-became-a-campf:
Irene Elliott Benson published How Ethel Hollister Became a Camp Fire Girl in 1912. Mrs. Hollister at first says no to the whole idea, in firm words. Ethel has home and school duties that fill all her time, she argues. She also knows, and likes, the friends Ethel keeps at present.

Camp Fire Girls was a new group for girls in those years. It taught outdoor skill, service, and friendship under a trained guardian. Ethel's path into the group forms the heart of the tale. Readers get a period story of mothers, daughters, and new freedom for girls.
21110-a-college-girl:
Darsie is chosen by an elderly aunt to live as her companion in Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's novel. The aunt coaches her in manners while a lively young family nearby gives Darsie company of her own age. Before dying, the aunt funds Darsie's great chance: a place at Newnham College, Cambridge.

The second half follows Darsie's student years, her friendships, and her final exams. She earns a Second rather than a First, enough to teach at a modest school. Her friend Dan takes First Class Honours and ends the book by asking her to marry him. Few novels of the time treated women's university study so fully.
22740-the-apple-dumpling-and-other-stori:
The Apple Dumpling and Other Stories for Young Boys and Girls is an old-fashioned storybook for children, built from simple tales of home and kitchen. The catalog record's credit line is garbled, and no year is given. Books of this kind taught reading and manners together, one small adventure at a time.

The title story follows its cook step by step: after paring the apples, she cuts each into four quarters. Then she fetches flour and a lump of butter from the cupboard, and carries a pitcher to the little spring close by for clear, cold water. The charm lies in the plain sequence, every errand named. Such stories let young readers rehearse the work of a household while following a dumpling to its fate.
24645-a-harum-scarum-schoolgirl:
Angela Brazil wrote this school story, published at New York in 1920 with pictures by John Campbell. Its heroine is Diana, a pixie girl and penniless princess, whose chapters include stars and stripes, a rush-bearing, Diana dares, French leave, and land girls. The story runs through Armistice Day and Diana's English Christmas.

Later chapters bring Diana to the rescue, Diana breaking out, Crusoe Island, spooks, joy-riding, and a family crest. Brazil's tale mixes schoolgirl fun, scrapes, and friendship in her best style. Young readers get a lively, old-fashioned school story, full of high spirits and kind hearts.
25145-a-patriotic-schoolgirl:
Angela Brazil's Patriotic Schoolgirl, published by Blackie and Son, is a wartime school story set at Brackenfield College. A new girl arrives at boarding school, joins dormitory life, and learns the school's customs, from exeats and autograph hunts to a talents tournament.

War soon touches the school through a Red Cross hospital, a secret society of patriots, patriotic gardening, and a roll of honor. Brazil, a prolific writer of school tales, mixes jokes, scrapes, and sentiment. The book captures how British schoolgirls were urged to do their bit during the First World War.
25765-a-dixie-school-girl:
Gabrielle E. Jackson writes A Dixie School Girl, published by Donohue in Chicago and New York in 1913, first volume of the Dixie Girl series. Jackson dedicates it to two Dixie neighbours whose childhood escapades helped make the stories.

Chapters open at full speed for Four Corners, where four straight country roads run at right angles. Woodbine follows, with Beverly Ashby squabbling good naturedly. A front picture asks Mr. Tedford for Huyler boxes, hinting at schoolgirl fun, sweets, and scrapes in a southern school story for girls. More Dixie Girl tales were promised after this first volume.
26061-the-gold-girl:
James B. Hendryx's western novel centers on Patty Sinclair, a ranch girl caught between rival men and a disputed claim. She rides the hills near the Watts ranch, crosses Monk Bethune, and draws a map that bears on the fight over gold. A horse raid, a found glove, and an unmasking push the plot toward her strike.

Lord Clendenning gets a ducking, the Bishop of All Outdoors passes through, and the tale closes with a race for the register. Patty's nerve drives the action: she takes precautions, faces down threats, and holds her ground in a camp where men expect her to fold. The book is a straight adventure of prospecting, ranch life, and frontier rivalry.
26986-the-ghost-girl:
H. De Vere Stacpoole's 1918 novel The Ghost Girl opens on a warm, grey Irish evening at Kilgobbin Park. Miss Berknowles reads in a window seat while rooks call over miles of parkland. The dusk blots out the country from Arranakilty to the Slieve Bloom Mountains.

A girl arrives who startles watchers with her likeness to Juliet Mascarene, a likeness in manner more than face, hinting at things hidden from the living. Stacpoole builds a quiet Irish ghost story of family resemblance, old houses, and the past pressing close behind the present.
27162-a-little-country-girl:
Susan Coolidge's A Little Country Girl, copyright 1885 and published by Roberts Brothers in 1895, follows Candace to the Narragansett country. The steamer Eolus pushes out from Wickford on a cool, brilliant June day, and the frontispiece shows Candace reading before breakfast at the staircase window.

Chapters take in a walk on the cliffs, the Manual of Perfect Gentility, a trip down to Beaver Tail, a talk about shyness, and two picnics. Marian's reading of directions for entering a room, hand stiff as a shingle, draws laughter and a gentle lesson in manners.
27363-burl:
Morrison Heady published this short work of fiction in Nashville with the Southern Methodist Publishing House in 1886, entered for copyright in 1884. Its preface asks to be read first, against the usual habit, because the author's own condition shapes how the book should be read.

Heady was both blind and deaf: for many years absolutely blind, and wholly without hearing. He spoke with singular clearness yet could receive word from others only through an alphabet carried upon his hand, spelled letter by letter. He argues that faith in the reality of a story matters to its enjoyment, and warns against breaking the illusion by dwelling on how it was written.
27839-only-an-irish-girl:
Mrs. Hungerford, writing as The Duchess, published Only an Irish Girl with the Prudential Book Company of New York. It opens in an Irish cottage, where Honor Blake laughs at her nurse Aileen's dream, and the old woman recalls Honor's dying mother at Donaghmore entrusting the child to her care.

The story sets Honor's love against family history: a suitor from a family that ground the poor and raised rents, whose father's sins, Aileen warns, visit the children. Romantic, sentimental, and Irish in voice, the novel belongs to the Duchess's popular late Victorian romances.
2787-an-old-fashioned-girl:
Louisa M. Alcott wrote this novel in two parts, the first in 1869, with a sequel demanded by beseeching little readers. Alcott's preface explains her purpose and apologizes for shortcomings with proper modesty.

Polly Milton, an old fashioned country girl, comes to the city and teaches her fashionable friends simplicity, kindness, and honest work. Alcott writes with warmth about growing up true in a world of show. The book endures as a beloved story of values that do not go out of style. Polly's plain dress outshines the city's finery. Polly stays true to the end.
27987-glory-and-the-other-girl:
Annie Hamilton Donnell published Glory and the Other Girl with the David C. Cook Publishing Company, a school story opening with Glory Wetherell running to bid her Aunt Hope good-by. Glory is miserable because she failed last year and must return to what she calls a baby seminary, while other girls enter Glenwood.

Aunt Hope, a thin little invalid on a big couch, teases Glory as her Little Disappointment, and Glory forgets her mileage book on the stairs. The novel follows a warm, impulsive girl through school, friendship, and growing up, in Donnell's affectionate manner for young readers.
28528-a-california-girl:
Edward Eldridge's A California Girl, published by the Abbey Press in 1902, addresses busy people rather than specialists. Its prologue names shop-girls, factory-girls, clerks, mechanics, farmers, merchants, and housewives as its readers. Eldridge weaves recent thought into story, hoping to help workers out of bondage in daily life.

Chapters follow Clara Lawton, the marriage of Charles Herne, Julia Hammond, Ben West, Stella Wheelwright, and Penloe. Ben West's Klondike experience, Penloe's sermon and original address, and a wedding in Orangeville carry the plot. Penloe joins the interior life of the Hindu to practical Western thought.
28989-the-biography-of-a-prairie-girl:
Eleanor Gates wrote this 1902 novel, The Biography of a Prairie Girl, published by the Century Company in New York. The book opens with the coming of the stork, a puzzle to the little girl. How did the bird reach a lonely Dakota farmhouse on a December afternoon without freezing? How did it carry her father away to a distant family? She remembers her christening and even earlier things, but never the wonderful journey itself.

Later chapters bring a frontier christening, Little Boy Blue, a pariah of the prairies, and a misfit scholar, through a harvest wedding, hard times, and the little teacher, toward the rising sun. Gates writes a prairie childhood with humor and tenderness. Readers get a beloved story of Dakota farm life, told as a girl grows from wonder to work.
29654-the-wall-street-girl:
Frederick Orin Bartlett's Wall Street Girl was printed in 1916 by Grosset and Dunlap with pictures by George Ellis Wolfe. It opens as Jonas Barton, senior member of Barton and Saltonstall, pauses over an interesting document to clean his glasses rather carefully, gaining time to think. Its chapters follow Don receiving a jolt, the need to eat, the queen in the parlor, and sandwiches. A picture warns Don that he lives too much downtown.

Bartlett writes a novel of finance, love, and the city, where a girl must hold her own among men of money. The tale mixes business with romance in the manner of its age. Readers of early business fiction will find a lively, period novel of Wall Street and the woman who braves it.
29753-the-gorgeous-girl:
Nalbro Bartley published The Gorgeous Girl in Garden City in 1920, with Doubleday, Page and Company. Trudy opens the tale by telling Mary Faithful that before long two bank accounts will beat as one, humming the wedding march as the office force listens. The O'Valley Leather Company is headed by its president, Steve O'Valley, and Mary serves him as private secretary and general guardian, so her say usually ends a dispute.

Trudy boards at the Faithful home and is irrepressible, while the Gorgeous Girl of the title has known nothing but the most gorgeous side of life. A get-rich-quick man, who always pays for his own speed, crosses the plot. Bartley keeps the office comedy brisk and the romance light. The book is a gay tale of work, money, and marriage in a busy firm.
30333-daddy-s-girl:
L. T. Meade tells Daddy's Girl, published by A. L. Burt in New York, with the epigraph, suffer the little children to come unto me. Meade, author of A Very Naughty Girl, Polly, A New Fashioned Girl, Palace Beautiful, Sweet Girl Graduate, and World of Girls, opens with Philip Ogilvie and his wife quarrelling. As their custom was, they quarrel in the drawing-room of the house in Belgrave Square, while the Angel in the nursery upstairs knows nothing about that.

Eight years old, the Angel decorates herself before the nursery looking-glass. At this moment, a quarrel between her father and mother threatens to embitter their whole lives and perhaps part them. Her lips are pursed in anxiety, her dark brows are raised, and her blue eyes fix on her own reflection. Shall it be buttercups, or daisies, or both, she thinks, with a box of flowers handy.
30630-a-guide-to-men-being-encore-reflec:
Helen Rowland writes A Guide to Men, subtitled Encore Reflections of a Bachelor Girl. Dodge Publishing issued it in New York in 1922, with a foreword by Fannie Hurst. Rowland says the material was gathered firsthand at considerable personal risk. It opens with a quip that a bachelor's life is one long solo, usually a hymn of thanksgiving.

The book is dedicated to Fannie Hurst, who found how to be happy though wedded to art and to a man at the same time. It moves through overture, prelude, refrain, bachelors, interludes, and true love, how to know it. Rowland offers witty, candid reflections on men, courtship, and marriage, in the voice of a sharp, modern bachelor girl.
31244-a-dear-little-girl:
Amy E. Blanchard's children's book, published by the Whitman Publishing Company of Racine, Wisconsin, follows eight-year-old Edna Conway, who dreads the word opportunity because it always seems to mean something unpleasant. When her parents must go to Florida for her mother's health, Edna is sent instead to Aunt Elizabeth's, where cousin Louis waits, a change of nests rather than a boarding school.

Thirteen chapters follow an accident, getting settled, Maggie's case, a guilty conscience, the fair, a wandering doll, a peck of trouble, adoption, a runaway, and pleasant changes. Gentle and old-fashioned, the story gives young readers a heroine learning to be brave in a new home.
31528-doubloons-and-the-girl:
John Maxwell Forbes's Doubloons and the Girl, published by Sully and Kleinteich with copyright in 1917, is a romance of treasure and adventure. Its contents open on the blind side of chance. They introduce Tyke Grimshaw and his affairs, and move through a hard hit, the shadow of romance, a setback, a broken chest, and a mysterious document. Later chapters promise the scourges of the sea, suggesting that the doubloons of the title are not easily won.

Forbes writes the popular adventure romance of his day, mixing a girl, a fortune, and the sea. The broken chest and the mysterious document give the plot its machinery, while chance and character decide the outcome. Readers of early twentieth-century popular fiction will find a lively, unpretentious tale of treasure hunting, where romance and risk sail together.
31700-reflections-of-a-bachelor-girl:
Helen Rowland's Reflections of a Bachelor Girl was published at New York by the Dodge Publishing Company, with copyright in 1909, and decorated by Henry S. Eddy. The book gathers short, sharp reflections on men, women, and matrimony, written from a bachelor's girl's point of view. One reflection pictures the average man treating matrimony as a hitching post where he ties a woman and leaves her until he comes home at night.

Another notes how joyfully a man pays a lawyer five hundred dollars to untie a knot he begrudged a clergyman fifty dollars to tie. Rowland's reflections are witty, unsentimental, and often unkind to male vanity, and they made her name as a humorist of the battle of the sexes.
31748-pemrose-lorry-camp-fire-girl:
Isabel Hornibrook's Pemrose Lorry, Camp Fire Girl, follows her books Drake of Troop One, Scout Drake in War Time, and Coxswain Drake of the Sea Scouts. Its first chapter, A Quaker Gun, opens with a Camp Fire girl of fifteen, nearly sixteen. She asks whether the Thunder Bird will really lay its egg upon the moon and drop a pound weight of steel on the Man in the Moon. Mammy Moon was the fairy foster mother of her childhood, the moon face she watched from her cot on wakeful nights.

The frontispiece shows a sky with not a remote sign of a biplane overhead. Hornibrook's book follows a Camp Fire girl whose fancy turns skyward, in a story of camp life and imagination.
32085-christine-a-fife-fisher-girl:
Amelia E. Barr's novel, published by D. Appleton and Company in 1917, follows Christine, a fisher girl of Fife on the Scottish coast. Its frontispiece shows her at the top of a cliff, turning to gaze again at the sea, and its epigraph declares that the sea belongs to God, who made it. Barr, already known for novels such as Joan and Profit and Loss, dedicated the book in January 1917 to a friend who, though a landsman, loves the sea.

The early chapters introduce the fishers of Culraine, Christine and the domine, and Angus Ballister, placing Christine inside a working fishing community. The sea shapes daily life, work, and risk for everyone around her. Readers get a period story of coastal Scotland, told through family, village custom, and a young woman's place in a trade ruled by weather, boats, and the catch.
32107-the-vision-of-elijah-berl:
Frank Lewis Nason's novel, published in Boston by Little, Brown and Company in April 1905, tells the story of Elijah Berl, a Californian guided by a vision. Its prelude paints the Pacific coast in broad strokes. Eight hundred and fifty miles of winding shoreline bend past gulls and barking seals on rocky islets. Mountains rise from the sea, and cattle herds with vaqueros gather around a bitter spring. Into that landscape Nason places a man with a mission disclosed to him point by point.

Berl deepens his springs and hoards the water they give, tending a cottage, a flower garden, and an irrigated orange grove under the San Bernardino mountains. He also shuts his ark against scoffers, holding to a vision that keeps him constant through depression. Readers get a California tale of faith, endurance, and a solitary purpose pursued while neighbours scoff.
32383-two-wyoming-girls-and-their-homest:
Carrie L. Marshall's girls' novel, copyrighted in 1899, follows two young women holding a homestead claim in Wyoming. Narrated in part by Jessie, the story opens in wind and rain as the girls manage a remote household and defend their land. Chapters follow a plot foiled, a visit from Mrs. Horton, a cattle brand dispute, a wildcat trail, and a chase by wolves.

Later episodes bring a storage reservoir, a queer bank, a missing man named Joe, and a long contest with Mr. Horton, who finally capitulates. The book mixes outdoor adventure with household resourcefulness, showing its heroines handling danger, neighbours, and paperwork with equal grit. It belongs to the era's stories of girls making a home and a living on the western frontier.
32429-the-mountain-girl:
Payne Erskine's novel, copyrighted in 1911 and 1912, opens with David Thryng arriving at Carew's Crossing and tasting the hospitality of mountain people. Aunt Sally departs and meets Frale, Cassandra brings David her trouble and her promise, and David later aids Frale's escape. Chapters follow Cassandra on an errand of mercy, a visit to Decatur Irwin's home, and spring in the mountains, when Cassandra tells David about her father.

Later David leases a farm, visits a bishop, and learns more of Cassandra's trouble, while Frale meets his enemy. The frontispiece promises a homeward walk together, hinting at the love story beneath the mountain action. Erskine writes warmly about rural manners, faith, and loyalty in a close-knit mountain community.
32949-the-american-country-girl:
Martha Foote Crow's American Country Girl, published in 1915 with fifteen photographs, is dedicated to the seven million country life girls of America. Crow wishes America's seven million farm girls to grasp their privilege and take up their share of country renewal. Crow asks first where the country girl is, then whether she is happy on the farm. Crow follows with stories of individual girls and chapters on work, inheritance, and the homesteader.

Later chapters turn practical, covering the household laboratory, efficient administration, and the new era Crow saw coming for rural women. The book is both a survey and an encouragement, arguing that country life could offer health, purpose, and standing if girls were trained and valued for it. As a document of the country life movement, it captures a moment when reformers tried to keep young women on the farm by making farm life better.
33208-the-laughing-cavalier-the-story-of:
Baroness Orczy's romance tells the story of the ancestor of the Scarlet Pimpernel, a laughing cavalier of an earlier age. Copyrighted in 1914, it opens with a prologue and an adventure on New Year's Eve, then moves through a fracas by a postern gate, watch-night, and the counsels of prudence. The hero, a swordsman with wit to match his blade, meets a painter, a Spanish wench, and foes who test his nerve.

Orczy, famed for the Scarlet Pimpernel, writes here with the same verve for disguise, daring, and romance. The tale is set in a world of inns, lodgings, and portraits, where a bargain or a portrait can turn a life. For readers who enjoy swashbuckling adventure with a light heart, the novel is a bright, fast-moving prelude to her most famous hero.
34226-the-iron-division-national-guard-o:
H. G. Proctor's 1919 narrative tells the story of the 28th Division, the Pennsylvania National Guard, in the World War. Its red keystone badge marked a Pennsylvania unit that earned a hard-won reputation for steady fighting during the second battle of the Marne in 1918.

Twenty chapters follow the men from home to the front, through the last German drive, the Vesle, and the Argonne, with chapters on air raids, ambulances, and a million-dollar barrage. Proctor writes as a unit historian, praising grit and naming the ground where the division fought. Proctor's chapters carry plain titles, from Men of Iron to Toward Hunland, tracking the division's road.
34484-waihoura-the-maori-girl:
Kingston wrote Waihoura, the Maori Girl, a tale of the first British settlers in New Zealand. An emigrant ship drops anchor in a port on the north island, and crowds of new folk rush to land with their goods. Clear sky, bold headlands, dark rocks, and tall woods frame the bay, with snow peaks far behind.

The new folk camp near the port in cottages, tents, and huts of boughs till they can take up the land they have picked. Young Valentine Pemberton, about eighteen, is glad to be safe at last on shore. The tale to come sets settler homes beside Maori life, with Waihoura at its heart. Kingston wrote many such tales of sea and new lands for boys.
35268-adventures-in-the-canyons-of-the-c:
James White and W W Hawkins wrote Adventures in the Canyons of the Colorado, two of its earliest explorers. William Wallace Bass added an introduction and notes. The authors published it at Grand Canyon, Arizona, in 1920. Bass is styled the Grand Canyon Guide. George Wharton James wrote the foreword. A hundred thousand now see the canyon yearly, James notes.

James sorts the canyon's famous men. Of all the crowds, only John Hance and Bass gained fame as guides, he says. Hance's fame rested on his exaggerated yarns alone, the Munchausen of the West. He was never a guide and knew nothing of the canyon twenty miles from his trail. The book prints the river tales of White and Hawkins under Bass's care.
36138-poppy-the-story-of-a-south-african:
Poppy: The Story of a South African Girl is a novel by Cynthia Stockley, printed at New York and London by Putnam's Sons in 1910. It was published in March of that year and reprinted again and again through October, twice in July alone. An old Irish legend gives the book its note on poppies: some say they are the tears of the moon, bringing forgetfulness and freedom from pain.

The heroine is Poppy Destin, aged nine. Pale as a witch, her light eyes are fierce with anger and disgust. She has slapped her little cousin Georgie for throwing a hammer that cut her leg. Her punishment is two boxes on the ear and no food all day. She throws the scraps to Nick the cat instead. The novel follows its hungry, defiant heroine out of that kitchen.
36853-a-very-naughty-girl:
Meade wrote a girls story printed at New York. Sylvia and Audrey opens the contents, then the arrival of Evelyn and the cradle life of Wild Eve. I draw the line at Uncle Ned and Frank's eyes follow. It is all detestable, one girl mutters within, and just when Evelyn is coming, too. I wish father would drop this horrid custom.

The hungry girl, staying to dinner, evening dress, and breakfast in bed fill the early chapters. Jasper was to go, I cannot alter my plans, and hunger come next. Jasper to the rescue, change of plans, and school lead to Sylvia's drive. The fall in the snow, a red gipsy cloak, and why did you do it raise the stakes. The torn book, stick to your colors Evelyn, one week of grace, and the loaded gun close a wild girl's taming.
37007-appropriate-clothes-for-the-high-s:
Appropriate Clothes for the High School Girl is a college bulletin by Virginia Alexander. She directed fine and applied art at the College of Industrial Arts, the state college for women at Denton, Texas. The bulletin treats a live question of its day: what schoolgirls should wear.

Alexander opens with a question put to her: why all this agitation on the subject of high school girls' dress? Interest, she answers, has grown for several years, and the girls themselves are directly responsible for it. The costumes worn to school have gone, she says, from bad to worse. Mothers and teachers have striven to correct matters, with little result. Only when the girls themselves saw the weakness and resolved to seek a cure did real results appear. Bulletins of this kind set standards of simplicity and sense in dress, and they belong to the history of home economics teaching in America.
37373-indian-scout-talks-a-guide-for-boy:
Indian Scout Talks is a guide for Boy Scouts and Camp Fire Girls by Charles Eastman, printed in nineteen fourteen. Eastman, a Dakota Sioux known as Ohiyesa, drew on his own early training. His chapters record first hand knowledge won before he was sixteen years old. The book is dedicated to the two youth movements named in its title.

Twenty six chapters teach the woodcraft of the Indian scout in plain lessons. They cover footprints, wild animals, and hunting with sling shot and bow. Canoes, camp sites, wigwams, and fire without matches follow in order. Blazed trails, signals, sports, and names with their meanings fill the middle. Ceremonies, gesture language, and picture writing serve both boys and girls. Weather wisdom, story telling, and wigwam manners close the course of talks.
37725-the-fisher-girl:
Bjornstjerne Bjornson wrote a tale Englished from the Norwegian by Sivert and Elizabeth Hjerleid and printed at London in 1871. The translators had Englished Ovind before, and offer this as a faithful copy of Bjornson's latest work. The poems keep the metre of the original, they say, and they have added headings to the chapters. Peer, Peter, and Pedro opens the book as the herring season stirs a coast town.

Some other boys, ready for confirmation, one and another, and a mistake follow. The sound of the clock, the first act, at the rural dean's, and fears fill the middle. Is music lawful, a chapter asks. Reconciliation and the scene close a tale of a fisher girl with a voice and a stage calling. Bjornson's warm peasants fill the small port.
39326-the-history-of-margaret-catchpole-:
The History of Margaret Catchpole, a Suffolk Girl is a novel by Richard Cobbold, first published in 1845. The World's Classics series at Oxford reprinted it with an introduction by Clement Shorter. Cobbold, born at Ipswich in 1797, is remembered, Shorter argues, as a man of one book.

The introduction notes that his other tale, Freston Tower, held the public for a time but has worn threadbare even in village libraries. Margaret Catchpole, meanwhile, survives as a classic in its way. The heroine was a native of the very district Cobbold served, so a romance lay ready to hand needing only passable writing to attract readers. How much of the story is truth and how much fiction, Shorter concedes, will never be known.
41136-a-plucky-girl:
Mrs L T Meade wrote a girls' novel copyrighted in 1900. The narrator, Westenra Wickham, was born a month after her father's death and named for him. His name was John Westenra Wickham, a strange name for a girl, she admits. Her mother loved the name and spoke of her father as if he were still living and close.

As a small child, Westenra's great treat was hearing tales of her brave father. Chapters ahead name Jane Mullins, paying guests, and a Berlin wool room. Her Grace of Wilmot enters the story. Ruin, a bond, and a duchess having her say all lie in wait. Meade writes in the first person throughout.
41545-the-orange-girl:
The Orange Girl, a novel by Sir Walter Besant, came out in 1898. Its title page shows Warren Davis as the hand behind its pictures. The tale is told in the first person by a man in debt gaol. He looks out from the King's Bench prison at the start. Chance of escape from that place looks slim to him then.

Chapter heads map a plot of plots in old London. A will is read, a claim is pressed, and an arrest falls. Newgate gaol, a masked ball, and a staged plot fill the mid part. A trial scene stands near the heart of the book. Jenny, the orange girl of the title, steers much of the action. Revenge bands and a fallen alderman close the long list.
42046-ireland-under-the-tudors-with-a-su:
Richard Bagwell wrote on Ireland under the Tudors in two volumes, with volume one printed at London in 1885. A short account of the earlier history goes with it. Irish policy, said Disraeli in the Commons, is Irish history, the preface quotes. I have no faith in any statesman who attempts to remedy the evils of Ireland while ignorant of the past, it runs.

History, to be of any use, should be written for instruction, Bagwell holds, and not merely to confirm existing prejudices. The writer who enters the arena as an advocate may produce an interesting party pamphlet, but he will hardly make the world wiser. The historian's true office is that of the judge. The reading public is the jury. Under that rule Bagwell marshals the facts of conquest, colony, and revolt. The colony proved too weak for its work, he finds early on.
43141-jill-a-flower-girl:
L T Meade wrote Jill, a Flower Girl, with illustrations by F H Townsend, published by Thomas Whittaker in New York in an edition dated eighteen ninety three. Chapter one opens in London at the height of the season. The weather was warm and sultry, and the days at their longest. Shops were gay with dresses, bonnets, gloves, and parasols. Night falls as the tale begins.

Before one of the largest mansions in Grosvenor Square a small crowd had collected, the tale says. Rough boys, eager pinched women, a few men, and even babies pressed for a peep inside. They jostled to reach the front rank and remarked freely on the folk going in, it adds. Among the watchers stands Jill, a poor flower girl whose life the rich house will cross. Girls get a London tale of poverty, pride, and kindness.
43145-the-squire-s-little-girl:
The Squire Little Girl, by L T Meade, was printed in London and Edinburgh in an edition dated 1902, with plates by Lewis Baumer. Meade opens at Harringay, where the Squire small daughter rides her pony down the drive. Village and rectory children press at the gate to stare.

The girl is Phyllis Harringay, age twelve, fresh come to live at the Hall. Her mother died at her birth, and her father lived abroad and took Phyllis with him. Now the Hall stands open, full of servants and guests, and Phyllis rides in full view. The watchers note a piquant yet dignified air in the small, erect figure. Girls of the day got a tale of rank, loss, and new friends at a country hall.
4345-sparrows-the-story-of-an-unprotecte:
Horace W. C. Newte wrote this novel about Mavis Keeves, an unprotected girl in Edwardian London. The contents follow the Devitts, Mavis's friends in need, her leaving the nest, barren ways, wider horizons, and a chapter called Spider and Fly. Later chapters bring a good Samaritan, surrender, springtime, and the way of all flesh.

Mavis moves through lodgings, work, prayer, and snares, with a nursing home and a new acquaintance late in the story. Newte's title points to his theme: a girl without shelter in a city of traps. The novel is frank for its time about poverty, temptation, and the small kindnesses that keep a young woman going.
44081-minnie-brown-or-the-gentle-girl:
Francis Forrester wrote Minnie Brown, or The Gentle Girl, a tale for children published in Boston in 1853. Forrester had earlier written Arthur Ellerslie and Redbrook. The book opens by asking why people call Minnie beautiful when her face is no prettier than many other girls' faces.

The answer is that Minnie's mind is beautiful. She has a lovely spirit, a mild temper, and a kind, obliging nature. She is never angry, unkind, or rebellious, and she speaks in a gentle voice with a pleasant smile. The story holds her up as a model for young readers, in the manner of Sunday school tales of the period. Its lesson is plain: true beauty lies in character, not in looks.
44362-the-adventures-of-harry-rochester-:
The Adventures of Harry Rochester is a boys' historical novel by Herbert Strang. Putnam issued the New York edition in 1905. William Rainey drew the illustrations. A motto from Bacon on honour heads the book. In a letter to a young reader, Strang states his aims. He means to tell a good story first of all. He also means to show a great British victory.

The tale is set in the days of Marlborough and Eugene. Those captains won fame in the Spanish Succession war. Strang draws on French staff histories for his facts. He also thanks Austin Dobson for period detail. Life and manners of two centuries past fill the scenes. Christ's Hospital boys are named as hoped-for readers. Strang's books taught history through adventure. This one joins a schoolboy hero to a famous campaign.
44847-a-little-candy-book-for-a-little-g:
A Little Candy Book for a Little Girl is a cookbook by Amy Waterman, printed at Boston in 1918 by the Page Company. Harriet O'Brien drew the colour frontispiece, and the book is given to Elizabeth and Dorothy. It stands in the Ideal Series for Girls beside little books on cooking, housekeeping, and sewing, each priced at seventy-five cents.

The contents open with cool weather candies, then popcorn goodies, fudge, caramels, and uncooked cream candies. A preface figure, Betsey Bobbitt, runs errands for neighbours who thank her with a penny for a stick of candy. Waterman writes in simple fashion, so a young cook can follow the processes of fudge, fondant, and nut dainties at home.
44848-a-little-preserving-book-for-a-lit:
A Little Preserving Book for a Little Girl is a story manual by Amy Waterman. The Page Company of Boston sold it in the Ideal Series for Girls. Each book in that cloth set cost one dollar in its day. Waterman's volume explains every step of preserving and canning in story form. Fruits and vegetables both come under her simple, clear teaching here.

Sister volumes teach cooking, housekeeping, candy making, and sewing to girls. A little girl home on Saturday mornings fills the housekeeping tale. Fudges, fondants, and nut dainties fill the candy book of the set. Books on vegetables, flowers, knitting, and nursing stood in preparation then. Adelaide and her friend Jessie May carry the preserving story along. A wonderful secret hinted in letters waits to be told between them.
44984-the-mystery-girl:
The Mystery Girl is a detective novel by Carolyn Wells, printed in Philadelphia and London by Lippincott in 1922. Wells had written Vicky Van and Raspberry Jam. She gives the book to Huber Gray Buehler, whom she calls a grave and reverend seigneur with a rare taste in mystery tales.

Chapters open with a president elect, then Miss Mystery arrives. Thirteen buttons, a broken teacup, and the tragedy follow. An incredible case, a volume of Martial, and the question where is Nogi pace the mid tale. A love letter, the spinster evidence, and Maurice Trask, heir, come late. Fleming Stone, Wells famed sleuth, enters at chapter fifteen. Miss Mystery own words and a planned elopement close the book. Mystery fans get a college town puzzle with a hidden name at its heart.
46467-the-remarkable-history-of-sir-thom:
The Remarkable History of Sir Thomas Upmore is a comic novel in a new edition of 1885, printed in London by Sampson Low. Its hero was formerly known as Tommy Upmore. A Horace tag about flying on no common wing stands on the title page. The preface is a small comedy in itself.

The narrator tells how Sir Thomas came and asked him to write a short account of his strange adventures. He declined the honour, having never seen the exploits. The history, he adds, flourishes by being more creditable, and far more credible, than that of England for the last few years. The refusal pained Sir Thomas, who is so bashful. And Sir Thomas's veracity, the preface swears, has become a proverb, even where his powers look supernatural. The tale that follows is tall, smiling fantasy.
48334-ireland-under-the-tudors-with-a-su:
Ireland under the Tudors, volume two, is a history by Richard Bagwell, issued at London in 1885. Bagwell's full title promises a short account of the earlier history as well. The second volume opens with the coming of Elizabeth to the throne. Its contents list runs chapter by chapter through the contests of the Irish chiefs and the English deputies sent to rule them.

Protestants rejoice at the new queen's accession, the first heads say. A dispute over the O'Neill succession follows, then a lord deputy and the restored Protestant rite. The parliament of 1560 and the royal supremacy in Ireland close the first chapter's list. Bagwell writes as a careful annalist, year by year, from state papers and records. His two volumes became a standard account of the Tudor conquest.
49742-the-battle-of-april-19-1775-in-lex:
The Battle of April 19 is a full tale of the first fight of the American war for free rule, by Frank Warren Coburn. It was made in a special small run at Lexington, with the muster rolls of the American bands that fought that day bound in. Each copy of that run bears its own print number.

Its front plate shows the British major by whose order the first volley of the war was fired. The tale takes in seven towns in turn, from the first shots at dawn to the long fight back to Boston. A note at the front tells how notes, slant text, and fixes from a list of known faults were set in this print form of the book.
50832-an-australian-girl:
An Australian Girl is a novel by Mrs Alick MacLeod, issued in an Australian edition of 1894. Bentley of London published it for the colonies only. A note marks the edition for Australian circulation. MacLeod also wrote The Silent Sea. The first chapter opens on a December Sunday. South Australia bakes under a still, hot sky.

The grass is withered almost to the roots. Dry ridges east of Adelaide bleach like carded flax. Gully shade still holds a faint grey-green. The tale promises days when the hall thermometer tops a hundred. Such heat shapes the lives on the page. Early Australian novels leaned on this harsh setting. Drought and distance test every character. MacLeod writes the hills with a settler's close eye. The book is a specimen of colonial fiction of its day.
50897-the-quest-of-the-golden-pearl:
Hutchinson wrote this adventure story, subtitled The Haunted Pagodas and The Quest of the Golden Pearl, illustrated by Hume Nisbet and published by Ward and Downey at London in 1897. Chapter one, The Shark-Charmer Walks the Plank, opens at the pearl fisheries of Ceylon.

The schooner Wellington rides at anchor at the northern end of the Strait of Manaar, on the famous pearl-fishing grounds, with the low Ceylon coast on her bow. Aboard are two boys. Jack is seventeen, sturdy and hot-headed, with a love of any row. His chum Roydon Leigh, called Don, is a year older, tall and canny. A quarrel breaks out among the native diving boats, which crowd together and then pull for the schooner before the signal gun. The captain is ashore, and Don holds command for the moment.
51495-the-uncensored-letters-of-a-cantee:
The Uncensored Letters of a Canteen Girl is a book of wartime letters published in New York in 1920. Henry Holt and Company issued it. The chapters are named for the French villages and the troops served in each. Company A, the doughboys, the artillery, and the engineers all appear.

The first letter is dated from Bourmont on November 24, 1917. The writer had just reached France and hoped for a red-roofed village. Bourmont, set sharply on a hill, granted that wish in full. She billets with an old couple in a steep lane of the town. The husband is a veteran of the Franco-Prussian War, wearing the Legion of Honour. Verdun and the French allies earn a chapter of their own near the end.
522-the-chinese-boy-and-girl:
Isaac Taylor Headland sketches Chinese child life for Western readers in this companion to his Chinese Mother Goose. He argues that no full study is possible while homes stay shut, yet streets, nurses, and shows offer rich glimpses. Rhymes, games, toys, and juggling fill the chapters.

Headland notes how Chinese toys match Western ones, and how nursery rhymes from many provinces echo Mother Goose. His aim is plain: to show Chinese children as real, human folk like any others. The book reads as a kind, curious bridge between East and West, told for families.
52713-ireland-under-the-tudors-with-a-su:
Richard Bagwell wrote Ireland Under the Tudors, a work in three books from London. Book three came out in 1890, past the first two by some years. Bagwell notes that the first parts were called a two book work by a slip. A third book had been pledged all along, and this book keeps that pledge.

This book deals with the revolts of Desmond and of Tyrone in full. It tells of the wreck of the Armada on Irish shores. The rash march of Essex and two landings from abroad get their due. A part tells of Captain Cuellar, a Spaniard cast on that coast. One part steps back to sketch life in the Ireland of Queen Elizabeth. Bagwell drew on state papers and on print works of his theme.
53249-the-laughing-girl:
Robert Chambers's The Laughing Girl was copyrighted in 1918 and issued by Burt at New York by arrangement with Appleton. Chambers dedicates it to his son Bob at Plattsburgh Barracks. A foreword in verse promises a tale of the beastly boche and the Bolsheviki, of lovers and villains, and asks readers safe in the guarded West to laugh in God's name. Twenty-five chapters begin with An Inheritance and move through a cellar, a pyjama party, and a mysterious Mister Smith.

A traveling circus, a countess, gangsters, and the Duchess of Naxos crowd the contents. The first chapter finds a deserted stone and timber chalet in a mountain valley, weeds smothering the garden, a red-headed slattern sweeping the veranda. Chambers, author of The Restless Sex and The Dark Star, writes a wartime romance of intrigue with a laughing heroine at its centre.
53386-the-flying-girl:
Edith Van Dyne wrote The Flying Girl, a novel of a girl who flies. The Reilly and Britton Company issued the book in Chicago in nineteen hundred eleven. Joseph Pierre Nuyttens drew the pictures. Van Dyne had won girls with her Aunt Jane’s Nieces tales.

The front note thanks Glenn H Curtiss and Wilbur Wright for their help. Orissa Kane is the heroine, a keen fan of flight. Her kin build the Kane aircraft in the tale. A bucking biplane and a flawed test raise the stakes. A spy named Tot Tyler pokes round the sheds. The last test and the big meet bring her hour. A fight in the air caps the plot. The close names the real heroine of the day.
5342-the-story-girl:
L. M. Montgomery's Story Girl follows a girl whose storytelling lights up a Prince Edward Island summer. Montgomery dedicates the book to her cousin Frederica E. Campbell, and it opens with Byron's lines on a form of life and light that, once seen, becomes part of sight, the morning star of memory.

The Story Girl herself, with her gift for tales, gathers cousins and neighbours around her, and Montgomery writes of orchards, lanes, and childhood summers with warmth. Readers who loved Anne will find here a companion novel, quieter and more reflective, about the girl who told the stories everyone remembered.
57166-just-a-girl:
Charles Garvice wrote Just a Girl, copyrighted in 1895 and issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Garvice was a best-selling writer of popular romance. This tale opens far from his usual drawing rooms, in Dan MacGrath's Eldorado Saloon at Three Star Camp, a mining settlement.

A lively row is on in the long, rough-boarded saloon. Miners and camp followers crowd the bar, the billiard table, and the faro table. Varley Howard, the professional gambler of Three Star and other camps, presides over the game. The camp took its name, the narrator jokes, from the legend on the brandy bottles. Garvice sets a story of love and chance in the rough West, where a girl's fate turns amid gold, gambling, and sudden fights.
57882-a-cruise-in-the-sky-or-the-legend-:
A Cruise in the Sky, or The Legend of the Great Pink Pearl, is by Ashton Lamar. The tale is the fifth volume of The Aeroplane Boys set. Reilly and Britton printed the set in Chicago. The series list shows the line: In the Clouds for Uncle Sam, The Stolen Aeroplane, The Aeroplane Express, and The Boy Aeronauts' Club stand before it. A sixth tale, Battling the Big Horn, follows.

The publisher's notice calls the stories the newest and most up to date, with all aeroplane details correct. Each volume came fully illustrated with a colored frontispiece, in cloth, at sixty cents. Lamar's tale takes the boy aeronauts cruising after a great pink pearl of legend. The set belongs to the first wave of aviation fiction for boys, when flight itself was still a wonder to sell a story.
58082-the-adventures-of-an-ugly-girl:
The Adventures of an Ugly Girl is a novel by Mrs George Corbett, issued as a semi-monthly number of a fiction series by Peter Fenelon Collier of New York. This copy is volume eleven, number ten, dated November 18, 1893, in a series sold by subscription at a dollar and a half. Corbett's other works crowd her title line: sea tales, wreck tales, and detective tales among them.

She wrote When the Sea Gives Up Its Dead, Adventures of a Stowaway, and The Mystery of Fellsmere. Her detective books include Adventures of an Amateur Detective and Adventures of a Lady Detective. The ugly girl's adventures thus come from a practised hand at sensation and mystery. The number as issued mixes the novel with the publisher's matter of the day, including a full-page advertisement for Beecham's Pills.
58099-mother-of-pearl:
Mother of Pearl is a set of tales by Anatole France, turned into English by Frederic Chapman. It was published in London by John Lane, the Bodley Head, in 1908. The book belongs to a full English edition of France's works.

The first and longest tale is The Procurator of Judaea. It tells of a Roman, Lamia, who was exiled by the emperor Tiberius on a charge tied to a consul's wife. Saints and sinners fill the pages that follow. Our Lady's Juggler and St Euphrosine stand beside Gestas, the thief of the cross. A village doctor's manuscript and the memoirs of a volunteer bring the set toward France's own day. The last tale is of a little leaden soldier.
60116-west-side-studies-boyhood-and-lawl:
West Side Studies holds two linked reports on poor youth in New York, Boyhood and Lawlessness and The Neglected Girl. Pauline Goldmark led the work. She had been a deputy head of the New York School of Philanthropy and sat on the state labour board. Ruth S True wrote the report on girls and shared in the boy study. A team of field staff helped with both parts.

Staff ran a Tenth Avenue club to watch and know the girls they describe. A mate volume, Mothers Who Must Earn by Katharine Anthony, is summed up at the start. Low pay for men, the intro says, drives worn wives out to earn as well. The studies hold that social ills link to each other and must be known as they are. Aid alone, they warn, is just a brief stop gap.
60457-when-i-was-a-little-girl:
Zona Gale wrote When I Was a Little Girl, tales of a small town childhood looked back on. The Macmillan Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred thirteen. Agnes Pelton drew its plates of scenes and dreams. Parts first ran under Curtis in nineteen hundred eleven.

Gale gives the book to the girl on Conant Street of old. Her grandmother Harriet Beers takes the memory half of the page. The lost girl still stirs at small signs, Gale writes. Sun on a floor, griddle cakes, or a town clock can wake her. Long hair, chatter, wild dreams, and faults are owned at once. The grown Gale now reads that child from deep within. Picnics, dolls, and a king’s trumpeter fill the bright scenes. Earth Mother and a great black hush close the fond set.
6334-sara-a-princess-the-story-of-a-nobl:
Fannie E. Newberry calls Sara a princess not by birth, for her title comes from above, her heritage is worth, and her empire is love. The story opens with a shrill voice up a steep, narrow stair, calling Sairay. A girl bent double over a book under a low roof raises her hands to her ears, then answers in a pleasant contralto. Her mother, hands in dough, wants nets mended at once, and Sara, sighing, marks her book and comes.

Omens good and ill, storm and trouble, a search and its ending follow, with Uncle Adam and Morton, Madame and the princess, happy days, and a tea party. News from the Nautilus, a fishing vessel on the Banks with a big haul and a superstitious captain, brings the sea into Sara's life. Newberry writes a girl's tale of duty, reading, and quiet nobility, where worth outranks birth.
64192-the-priceless-pearl:
Alice Duer Miller wrote The Priceless Pearl, a novel. Dodd, Mead and Company issued it at New York in 1924. Miller had written Manslaughter before this. Come Out of the Kitchen bears her name. Chapter One opens in an office at once. Bunner, the office manager, complains in it.

The girl is simply too good-looking, Bunner says. She works hard, thinks fast, and keeps good manners. Her looks disturb the office all the same, he holds. He made a grave mistake in hiring her, he says. The president is a trifle deaf in the scene. He was a botany professor before this post. He heads an encyclopedia publishing house now. Mr Rixon, third vice president, is crying, Bunner tells him. Rixon has fallen in love with the girl. A comedy of beauty at the office mines Miller's wit on work, men, and the perils of a pretty typist.
64279-test-for-the-pearl:
Test for the Pearl, a science fiction story by Vaseleos Garson, was printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1947. Together, an Earthman and a Jovian have outfought prison guards, a Venusian jungle, and the cunning Chameleon men. Together they were invincible, its headnote says. But at the Test for the Pearl they divided.

The story opens as an escape siren roars over the Interplanetary Prison on Venus. Chameleon men halt in the steaming jungle at the sound, and Earth patrols break into a run. Near the prison wall a patch of ground quivers once and lies still, hiding the fugitives. The Jovian Waltk lies beside the Earthman, warned to keep still for hours. Garson builds a tale of escape, alien friendship, and a final trial that tests the pair against each other.
65386-the-little-french-girl:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick wrote The Little French Girl, held in 1924 at Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin. Sedgwick had writ Adrienne Toner and Christmas Roses. Four impressions ran by September 1924. Part One opens as a clock strikes eight in a London station. Alix, the little French girl, counts the strokes in the fog.

The strokes seem to glide downwards rather than fall, Alix thinks. They make her think of tawny drones pushing forth from hot thyme in the garden at Montarel. She sits straight in her corner of the Victoria waiting room. She fixes her mind on that picture so she shall not feel too sharply what the hour means. Nothing could be more unlike Montarel than this cold, paltry scene, she holds. Sunlight and silence there stand against dense air and tumult here.
67410-our-winnie-and-the-little-match-gi:
Evelyn Everett Green wrote Our Winnie and The Little Match Girl, two tales for young readers in one book. John F Shaw and Company in London issued the volume. Green had written The Master of Fernhurst, In Cloister and Court, and other tales. Our Winnie holds nine chapters. The Little Match Girl holds six chapters. Winifred, called Winnie, is the heroine of the first tale.

Winnie sits by a nursery window and watches swallows in a rosy sunset sky. The great round window looks on garden, hedge, fields, and a lake that shines like gold. A plate notes that the child knows her bird friends will soon fly far away. Trouble, a strange journey, and a party shape her tale. The second tale starts with a small match seller and moves to a studio and to Brooklands. Both tales mix pathos and hope for young hearts.
67865-the-samovar-girl:
The Samovar Girl is a Siberian adventure novel by Frederick Moore, author of Sailor Girl and Siberia To-Day, published by Appleton at New York and London in 1921. Moore dedicates the book to Robert Davis.

A prologue in a valley of despair gives way to chapters set twenty years after: an intelligence officer, a firing squad, and the place of the vow. Then come the ataman's decision and the prison on the hill. Peter lays his plans, Ilya uses his wits, an American comes, and Katerin plans to meet him before the trap shuts and the final reckoning arrives. The opening scene is all chains: a column of prisoners from the big prison swings down the road toward the taiga to cut wood under Cossack guard.
68069-the-principal-girl:
The Principal Girl is a tale of the gay world by Snaith, put out at New York in nineteen twelve with all rights held. The same hand's past tales are list at the front, with names of wives, maids, and young men of rank. The list of parts is writ in a jest tone from the first head to the last.

A great state lord in a far land heads the first part, with more such great sights. One part treats a theme of grave weight for the state, and the next is of the home, yet, it hopes, not past the worth of a great man of law. The dear reader is then made known to the seventh unwed daughter of not quite a mint of earls.
69191-the-cave-girl:
The Cave Girl is a novel by Edgar Rice Burroughs, printed at New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1925. Burroughs also wrote Tarzan and the Ant Men, The Land That Time Forgot and Pellucidar. The book is in two parts. The first part's chapters run from Flotsam to Capture. The second part takes in King Big Fist, The Great Nagoola, The Abduction of Nadara and The Rescue.

The hero is Waldo Emerson Smith-Jones, a young man reared in a rich Back Bay home. He was taught to look down on strength of body as gross and primitive. The front picture shows the cave girl saving Waldo's life. Her name is Nadara, and the tale follows the weak city man among the wild people of the island.
69912-the-popish-plot-a-study-in-the-his:
The Popish Plot, by John Pollock, is a study of the plot panic in the reign of Charles the Second. Pollock was a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, and Duckworth printed the book in London in 1903. He inscribes it to the memory of Lord Acton.

Three quotes head the work, and the first sets its method. Some truth there was, it runs, but dashed and brewed with lies. A table of events in the plot's history stands before the text. The first part treats the designs of the Roman Catholics, with Titus Oates at its heart. The second follows Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey, with the informers Bedloe and Prance. Politics fills the third part: the government, the Catholics, Shaftesbury, and Charles. Trials for treason close the book, with chapters on the judges and on criminal procedure.
702-somebody-s-little-girl:
Martha Young wrote this tale for children about Bessie Bell, a little girl who half-remembers a strange green country that grown folk say cannot exist. She recalls a window that looks out on a world always moving and changing, and a small red apple that stirs her heart. Adults tell her such things are not real, so she keeps her wonders to herself.

The story follows Bessie as memory, dream, and daily life blur, and as she learns to trust what she feels. Young writes in a soft, dreamy voice, close to a child's own thought. The book charms readers who recall how childhood fancy can feel truer than fact, and it stands as a gentle piece of early American fantasy for the young.
71255-the-green-girl:
Jack Williamson wrote a serial in two parts that ran in Amazing Stories in March and April 1930. Wesso drew the pictures. At high noon on May 4, 1999, the sun went out, the tale opens. It had risen bright and clear. A recent issue of Science and Invention told of Doctor Hartman's diving bell discoveries off Sicily, the editor notes, a prehistoric city found below the sea, perhaps lost Atlantis.

Why then should there not be cities, even vast cities, submerged miles below the Pacific and made habitable, he asks. The Green Girl is a scientifiction classic that will rank with the best ever published, he cries, wild and fantastic yet exceedingly plausible. The narrator had risen at dawn for a plunge in the surf and walked a strip of virgin woodland in peace. Then the light failed. Williamson's first fame rests on this tale.
7231-light-o-the-morning-the-story-of-an:
L. T. Meade's Light o' the Morning follows an Irish girl named Nora through chapters that mix home trouble, wild neighbours, and school discipline. The Murphys, the squire's trouble, the cave of the banshee, and a diamond cross mark her path. A feather-bed house and a rose-coloured dress join them, while letters, telegrams, and ten pounds turn the plot at sharp moments.

Meade writes for young readers with a brisk, kindly eye, letting Nora's cheek and spirit carry her through scoldings and small adventures. The story balances Irish country life with the taming lessons of school, and its heroine grows steadier without losing her fire. The title's morning light suits a tale of youth finding its way.
73572-the-shadow-girl:
Ray Cummings wrote The Shadow Girl, a book length science fiction novel reprinted in Science Fiction Quarterly in spring nineteen hundred forty two. Smolenski drew the pictures. The blurb calls Cummings a prime name in the field. Folk from far time strike back at a famed doctor in the tale.

Alan and his friend Ed set up a new color television set at night. Alan’s sister Nanette models a clay figure as they work. No known station will tune in on the screen. Then a dim shape forms in pale star light. A girl’s shade stands in a purple sky of mist. Fear grips the three as they watch. The set has caught a call from years yet to come.
73780-the-other-miller-girl:
The Other Miller Girl is a novel for girls by Joslyn Gray, published by Scribner at New York in 1922. Gray had written Bouncing Bet, The January Girl, and Rosemary Greenaway in the same shelf. A front picture shows a girl at a door saying she is so sorry, but they do not have company, you know. Gray dedicates the book to a Florence, in memory of Toddie and the days before a birthday.

The story opens on a pleasant Saturday afternoon in late September, after the awarding of the Wadsworth prize, as Mr Langley receives three visitors. The church at Farleigh, an old fashioned New England meeting house with perfect proportions, stands in the tale's world. Gray writes of sisters and mistaken standing in a small town.
7493-the-daughter-of-the-chieftain-the-s:
Edward S. Ellis wrote this frontier story for young readers, set in the Wyoming Valley between the Blue Ridge and the Allegheny Mountains, where the Susquehanna River runs through. The opening chapter introduces Omas, Alice, and Linna. It begins, oddly and charmingly, with the game of jackstones. The little rubber ball is tossed in the air, and the iron prongs are caught one by one, then two at a time, then three and four.

From that playground start, the story follows the daughter of a chieftain through the dangers and loyalties of the frontier valley. Ellis, a veteran writer of boys' adventure, keeps the tale swift and clear, explaining the country as he goes. The book offers young readers an old-fashioned Indian story, told with sympathy for its heroine and love for the valley she calls home.
75934-a-little-irish-girl:
A Little Irish Girl is a novel by J M Callwell, author of A Champion of the Faith, printed at London and Glasgow. Its first chapter is set at the Miss Clarksons' educational establishment for young ladies. For some dozen years the school had been owned by three middle-aged sisters, the Miss Clarksons, principals of a large and flourishing school.

Their house, Treherne House, stands in a northern suburb of London. In the middle of the last century it was a stately family mansion. A broad flight of stone steps leads to the hall-door, and iron extinguishers by the railings recall the linkboys who put out their torches after escorting ladies home. The chapters move to Cousin Ansey's legacy, Norah's freak, and Moyross Abbey. A ghost in the monk's walk, an oration by Malachy, and a vision of the past follow.
76268-the-sea-girl:
Ray Cummings wrote The Sea Girl, a serial from Argosy All-Story Weekly in the spring of 1929. Its blurb warns of sunken ships and strange ocean changes. Those signs, it says, presage the mightiest threat ever made against man's world. The tale opens in March 1990, with a sea disaster that drew scant note at the time. An old freight ship sank in mid-Pacific, with the loss of all on board.

Geoffry Grant, age twenty-two, was among the first to hear the distress call. He was chief officer of the largest vessel of the Sub-Pacific Freighters line. Grant tells the tale in his own voice, from that first call on. A line at the head speaks of a golden palace at the bottom of the sea. Cummings mixes sea lore, future craft, and a siren's mystery in one fast serial.
76490-the-sea-girl:
Marguerite Aspinwall wrote a tale of Nantucket in the clipper ship days, copyrighted in 1928. Ralph D Dunkelberger drew its pictures. The book is dedicated to Alice Low Sand. She first taught the author to know and love Nantucket, the dedication says. A picture caption gives the heroine's creed. If I can't be a boy and go to sea, she says, the next choice would be a tern or a great gray gull. Harper published the novel at New York and London.

Nantucket's whaling and clipper past frames the girl's longing. Aspinwall wrote for girls who chafed at shorebound lives. The sea girl watches ships and gulls from the island. Historical girls' fiction of the twenties often gave its heroines such yearnings.
78471-beryl-and-pearl:
Beryl and Pearl is a novel for girls by Agnes Giberne, here in its fourth edition from Nisbet in London. Giberne wrote improving fiction for young readers, and the motto verses promise reverent listening love and daily work prepared by faith. The contents follow three sisters through school life, confirmation, ill tidings and a decision.

The book opens with Mr Josiah Crosbie, a ruddy, gouty and impatient old gentleman, rapping his stick on the study door and shouting for Millicent. Millicent Cumming, his widowed niece of thirty-two, answers in an unhurried silver voice from the garden door. Her Madonna-like calm, the narrator notes, carries lines that tell of tempests past. Beryl and Pearl, the younger sisters of the title, are to be formed under that calm. The novel is Victorian evangelical domestic fiction, built on trials of patience and the training of character.
78662-the-type-writer-girl:
The Type-Writer Girl is a novel by Olive Pratt Rayner, printed at London by Pearson in 1897. The book is inscribed to the author's husband and brother. Twenty two chapters tell the tale. Two chapters are named for Romeo, and a late one is called I Cling to the Rigging.

The chapter titles sketch her road: the struggle for life, the choice of a patron, a drawn battle, an autumn holiday. One title jokes that now Barabbas was a publisher, and another shows her trying literature herself. The tale belongs to the wave of novels of the 1890s about the New Woman at work. It treats her job, her lodgings, her friends and her loves with a light hand. The book is a fair window on the first age of the woman typist in London.
79694-bad-girl:
Bad Girl is a novel by Vina Delmar, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York. Harcourt, Brace held the copyright in 1928. Seventeen printings ran from April 1928 to March 1929. That list fills a full page of the front matter. The dedication is to Gene, who waited downstairs. Part one opens aboard a famous excursion steamer at night. Some one had brought a ukulele to the boat. Its player hits the strings with a gay discordancy. A falsely keyed voice follows the last chord with a long note.

High feminine laughter completes the grotesque performance, Delmar writes. The steamer Burma glides on through the shining Hudson night. She seems to toss her head at the private boats. Delmar's tale of a working girl's love was a best seller. Its plain speech about young city lives made its fame.
9858-star-dust-a-story-of-an-american-gi:
Fannie Hurst's 1921 novel tells the story of Lilly Becker, an American girl with talent and ambition. It opens with Lilly at the piano, working through Rubinstein's Melody in F, while her young mind reaches for something larger than her daily life.

Book One, called The Vine, follows her growth as she seeks a place in the world through music and will. Hurst writes warmly about family, work, and a woman's hopes in early twentieth-century America. Readers get a heartfelt portrait of a girl determined to make her gifts count.
a-little-cook-book-for-a-little-girl: Caroline French Benton writes a little cook book for a little girl. Dedicated to Katherine, Monica, and Betty, three girls who love little girl cooking, it reprints most of its matter from Good Housekeeping. Recipes begin with cereals for breakfast, cooked the night before. Benton teaches young cooks in plain steps they can follow safely.
