a-popular-schoolgirl: Angela Brazil tells a girls' school story centred on Wynch-on-the-Wold, opening with the end of the holidays and the bustle of opening day. The chapters follow an intruder named Bess, a fifth-form fete, a school parliament, hockey, a hostel frolic, and the whispering stones. Through strikes, rivalries, and an Easter pilgrimage, the book celebrates schoolgirl loyalty, mischief, and the small parliaments by which young people govern themselves.
an-old-fashioned-girl:
Louisa May Alcott explains her plan in her preface. The first part of her story was written in 1869. Readers' begging letters then forced a sequel. It carried her heroine six or seven years forward. Polly Milton, a country minister's daughter, arrives in the rain to visit the fashionable Shaw family in the city. Her plain dress and plain manners startle them.

The first chapters — Polly Arrives, New Fashions, Polly's Troubles, Grandma — show her goodness quietly shaming city vanity. Six years afterward, the children are grown, fortunes have changed, and Polly, now a music teacher, holds the family's respect. Alcott writes a moral tale without sourness, full of household detail and warm humor.
apples-ripe-and-rosy-sir-and-other-stori: Mary Catherine Crowley gathers a set of short tales for young readers, opening with a March story in which late snow gives children one more round of sledding and skating. Later pieces turn on boat building, a May Day gift, a plain white dress, a miser's gold, and a red silk frock. Each tale pairs a small domestic scene with a plain moral choice, often about kindness, thrift, or truth. The tone stays warm and direct, and the stories suit reading aloud to children or early independent readers.
brentano-geschichte-vom-braven-kasperl-u:
Honest Kasperl loves beautiful Annerl, and rigid codes of honor crush them both. Brentano's Geschichte vom braven Kasperl und dem schoenen Annerl, his most famous story, appears here in German. Told with folk-ballad simplicity, the tale works like a song everyone in the village already knows.

A frame narrator hears the double tragedy from an old grandmother, which deepens its ache. Questions of guilt, shame, and a soldier's honor turn private love into public ruin. The story devastates quietly, without a wasted scene. German readers have cherished it for two centuries as a classic of the novella. Its plain style hides how carefully every detail is placed.
britannica-1911-achard-franz-carl:
Franz Carl Achard (1753-1821) was a Prussian chemist born at Berlin who turned a laboratory discovery into an industry. His predecessor Marggraf had found sugar in beetroot, and Achard made that finding practical. By about 1800 he was producing beet-sugar in considerable quantities at Kunern in Silesia, on an estate the king of Prussia granted him, though his process was still imperfect.

Teaching spread the method. At Kunern he also ran a school of instruction in sugar manufacture with an international reputation. For a time Achard directed the physics class of the Berlin Academy of Sciences. His chemical and physical researches filled several published volumes, and his discoveries included a method of working platinum.
britannica-1911-begas-karl:
Karl Begas, who lived from 1794 to 1854, was a German painter of history born at Heinsberg near Aachen. The 1911 Britannica article says his father, a retired judge, meant him for the law. The boy's bent ran hard to art. At school his skill with the pencil was already marked. In 1812 he was let go to Paris to train. He worked for eighteen months in the studio of Gros.

In 1814 the king of Prussia bought his copy of a famed Madonna. The king backed him from then on. Begas painted large scenes from the Bible for churches in Berlin and Potsdam. He was famed as well for portraits, and gave the royal gallery a long row of Prussian men of letters. At his death he held the post of court painter at Berlin. His son Oskar followed him as a painter and teacher there.
britannica-1911-biedermann-friedrich-kar:
Friedrich Karl Biedermann (1812–1901) was a German publicist and historian, born at Leipzig. He studied at Leipzig and Heidelberg. In 1838 he became a professor at Leipzig University. His early books argued strongly for German unity. He sat in the Frankfort national parliament of 1848. In Saxony's upper house he backed union under Prussian leadership. That stand cost him his professorship for a time.

He edited newspapers at Weimar and then back at Leipzig. He regained his chair in 1865, the 1911 Britannica entry notes. He sat in the German Reichstag from 1871 to 1874. His chief works include memoirs of the Paulskirche assembly and a history of Germany from 1815 to 1871. He also wrote a cultural history of the German people and three historical dramas. He died at Leipzig in March 1901.
britannica-1911-brugsch-heinrich-karl:
Heinrich Karl Brugsch (1827–1894) was a German Egyptologist born in the barracks at Berlin on 18 February 1827, son of a Prussian cavalry officer. He showed a great inclination to Egyptian studies early and, though encouraged by Humboldt, was almost entirely self-taught. After his university course and visits to foreign museums, the Prussian government sent him to Egypt in 1853, where he formed a close friendship with Mariette.

On his return he took a post in the Berlin museum. A special mission to Persia under Baron Minutoli followed in 1860, and after Minutoli's death Brugsch discharged the ambassador's functions. Consul at Cairo in 1864, professor at Gottingen in 1868. In 1870 director of the school of Egyptology founded at Cairo by the khedive, he was unceremoniously dismissed in 1879 by European controllers bent on economising. French influence kept him from succeeding Mariette at the Bulaq Museum in 1883, and he lived mainly in Germany until his death on 9 September 1894.
britannica-1911-cadogan-william-cadogan-:
William Cadogan, first Earl Cadogan, lived from 1675 to 1726 and was a British soldier. The 1911 Britannica life makes him son of Henry Cadogan, a Dublin barrister. His grandfather had governed Trim in Ireland in his own day. The family claimed descent from Cadwgan, an old Welsh prince of lore. William began his army life as a cornet of horse under William the Third.

He fought at the Boyne and in the Low Countries with his regiment. In those years he caught the eye of the great Marlborough. In 1701 Marlborough took him as a staff officer for hard tasks. Soon he was that captain's trusted right hand man in war. His work in 1701 won him a regiment of horse of his own.
britannica-1911-cairns-hugh-mccalmont-ca:
Hugh McCalmont Cairns, first Earl Cairns (1819-1885), was an Irish statesman and lord chancellor of England, and this 1911 Britannica entry traces his slow start at the bar. He was born at Cultra in County Down. He was schooled at Belfast academy and at Trinity College, Dublin, taking a high degree in classics in 1838. In 1844 he was called to the bar at the Middle Temple.

In his first years at the chancery bar he showed little sign of the eloquence that later marked him. He spoke so slowly and with such shyness that he feared the fault might wreck his career. In time he shook off that fear. In 1852 he entered Parliament as member for Belfast, and in 1856, on becoming a Queen's Counsel, his inn made him a bencher.
britannica-1911-cathcart-william-schaw-c:
William Schaw Cathcart, first earl Cathcart, lived from 1755 to 1843. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows the soldier and envoy. He was born at Petersham in September 1755 and schooled at Eton. His father was then ambassador at Saint Petersburg for Britain.

Cathcart studied law, then took a cavalry post in 1776. In America he won field promotion twice in one campaign. He led an irregular corps called the British Legion with success. Home posts and Low Country wars raised him step by step. He led the British force sent to Hanover in 1805. Two years later Copenhagen surrendered to his expedition in Denmark. An earldom followed his work with allied chiefs in 1814. He had kept many proud generals in harmony through that war.
britannica-1911-churl:
Churl comes from the Anglo-Saxon ceorl, kin to the German Kerl, and names one of the two main classes of early Anglo-Saxon freemen. The other class was the eorl, and in time the ceorl's status probably sank, though his political power was never large. Before the Norman Conquest he can hardly be classed among the unfree, the entry argues. He often held land, held some position and could rise to the rank of a thegn.

Except in Kent his wergild was fixed at 200 shillings, one sixth of a thegn's, making him the twyhynde man of Anglo-Saxon law. After the Conquest the ceorls sank into servitude, and the word renders the villanus of Domesday Book. The form passed through cherl in Chaucer and others toward churl. Sense then slid from man and husband to peasant, and at last to a low, surly or miserly person.
britannica-1911-cowper-william-cowper-1s:
William Cowper, first Earl Cowper (about 1665–1723), was lord chancellor of England. He was the son of Sir William Cowper of Ratling Court in Kent. His father sat in parliament as a Whig of some mark in the last Stuart reigns. The son was schooled at Saint Albans and called to the bar in 1688. He gave his loyalty to the prince of Orange at his landing.

A large practice at the bar backed his rise in the House. Men rated him among the most effective speakers of his generation. In 1702 he lost his seat on a tide of ill will. His brother Spencer had stood trial on a charge of murder, and the stain spread. In 1705 he became lord keeper of the great seal. He took his seat on the woolsack without a peerage. Talks for the union with Scotland filled the next year.
britannica-1911-cromer-evelyn-baring-1st:
Evelyn Baring, 1st earl of Cromer (born 1841), was a British statesman and diplomatist born on 26 February 1841. He joined the Royal Artillery in 1858 and served as aide-de-camp in the Ionian Islands. In 1872 he went to India as private secretary to his cousin Lord Northbrook, the viceroy. In 1876 he became British commissioner of the Egyptian public debt office. His searching report on the Khedive Ismail's finances followed in 1878.

After Ismail's forced abdication in 1879, Baring became British controller-general under the Dual Control. He spent 1880 to 1883 as finance member of council in India. In 1883 he returned to Egypt as British agent and consul-general. The body of the entry follows his long tenure there and weighs its results. It closes with his two-volume Modern Egypt, an account of events in Egypt and the Sudan since 1876. At home he joined the free-trade wing of the Unionist party.
britannica-1911-elze-karl:
Elze, Karl (1821–1889), was a German scholar and Shakespeare critic born at Dessau on 22 May 1821. He studied classical philology and modern, above all English, literature at Leipzig from 1839 to 1843. For a time he taught at the Gymnasium at Dessau. In 1875 he became extraordinary professor, and in 1876 full professor, of English philology at Halle, where he died on 21 January 1889.

Elze began his writing career with the Englischer Liederschatz of 1851, a gathering of English lyrics, and edited for a while a critical journal called Atlantis. In 1857 he published an edition of Shakespeare's Hamlet with critical notes. He also edited Chapman's Alphonsus and wrote lives of Walter Scott, Byron, and Shakespeare. His Abhandlungen zu Shakespeare appeared in English as Essays on Shakespeare in 1874. The entry praises his Notes on Elizabethan Dramatists, three volumes printed at Halle from 1880 to 1886, for its guessed corrections of the text.
britannica-1911-fitzwilliam-william-went:
English statesman William Wentworth Fitzwilliam, second Earl Fitzwilliam, born in seventeen forty eight, opens a family account in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was son of the first earl, who died in seventeen fifty six. The family claimed descent from a son of William the Conqueror.

An early member bought the family seat at Milton in Northamptonshire in fifteen oh six. Later kin won Irish and English titles over many years. A separate Irish branch is set apart from the Milton house. Its best known man left a library and funds for a museum at Cambridge. The second earl gained the Fitzwilliam lands, and in seventeen eighty two he also gained rich lands from his uncle, the Marquess of Rockingham.
britannica-1911-gilbert-grove-karl:
Grove Karl Gilbert (1843- ) was an American geologist, born at Rochester, New York, on the 6th of May 1843. This 1911 Britannica article notes that he joined the Geological Survey of Ohio in 1869. In 1879 he became a member of the United States Geological Survey, working in parts of the Rocky Mountains and in Nevada, Utah, California, and Arizona.

Gilbert won note for his studies of mountain structure, the Great Lakes, glacial action, and recent movements of the earth. His report on the Henry Mountains in 1877 first set out the volcanic form known as a laccolite. His works on the Niagara River and on Lake Bonneville are singled out as of special weight, and he won the Wollaston medal from the Geological Society of London in 1900.
britannica-1911-goldmark-karl:
Karl Goldmark, a Hungarian composer born in 1832, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Keszthely on Lake Balaton, the son of a poor cantor in the local Jewish synagogue. The house was full of music all the same. The boy played a cheap violin and a flute he made from reeds cut at the river bank.

A village schoolmaster helped him into a music school, and in 1844 he went to Vienna to study the violin. War drove him to a band post at Raab, where he was near shot as a spy. Back in Vienna he turned to composing. A concert of his own works in 1857 made his first quartet a talking point. Overtures named Sakuntala and Penthesilea came next and showed the mark of Wagner.
britannica-1911-goodwin-nathaniel-carl:
Nathaniel Carl Goodwin, an American actor born in Boston in 1857, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. While a clerk in a large shop, he studied for the stage. He made his first appearance in 1873 in Boston, as a newsboy in a play in Stuart Robson's company. He scored at once with his imitations of popular actors.

A hit in a burlesque led Goodwin into an Evangeline company, and he wed the English actress Eliza Weathersby. Not till 1889, though, was his talent as a comedian of the legitimate type recognized. From then he appeared in plays built to show his dry humour. They included A Gold Mine, A Gilded Fool, Nathan Hale and When We Were Twenty One. Till 1903 he performed with his third wife, the actress Maxine Elliott, whom he had wed in 1898.
britannica-1911-granville-granville-geor:
Granville Leveson-Gower, second Earl Granville, is set out in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London in 1815, he was the first earl's eldest son. His father had served as envoy at St Petersburg and at Paris. Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, gave the young lord his schooling. A short stay in Paris under his father came after that.

In 1836 Leveson entered parliament for Morpeth in the Whig cause. A brief post as under-secretary for foreign work came to him next. In 1840 he wed Lady Acton, a widow of Dalberg stock. Till 1846 he sat for a new seat while his father lived. That year his father's death brought him the earldom and its weight. His long role in Liberal state work starts from that year.
britannica-1911-granville-john-carteret-:
Granville, John Carteret, Earl, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an English statesman. Born on the 22nd of April 1690, he was known for much of his life as Lord Carteret. His kin came from the Channel Isles and were of Norman stock. He was schooled at Westminster and at Christ Church, Oxford.

Swift is quoted as saying Carteret took away more Greek and Latin than fit his rank. He kept a love of the old tongues all his life. He also knew modern tongues well, and was rare in his day for knowing German. He wed in 1710 and took his Lords seat in 1711. Though his kin had backed the Stuarts, he stood firm for the Hanover line.
britannica-1911-grey-charles-grey-2nd-ea:
Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey (1764-1845), was an English statesman, born at Fallodon near Alnwick on 13 March 1764. The 1911 Britannica entry sets his career against his father's. General Sir Charles Grey, later the 1st Earl, served nearly fifty years, from Minden to the capture of Martinique and Guadeloupe.

The son made verses at Eton while his father fought the American colonists. As young member for Northumberland he denounced Pitt's war on revolutionary France. While Napoleon threatened invasion, the father commanded the southern district and took his earldom in 1806. The long article follows the son's own half-century in politics: long opposition, then the premiership that carried the Reform Bill of 1832. That act, and the abolition of slavery that followed, fixed his place in English history.
britannica-1911-grey-henry-grey-3rd-earl:
Henry Grey, 3rd Earl Grey (1802-1894), was an English statesman, born on 28 December 1802, son of the 2nd Earl Grey of Reform Bill fame. The 1911 Britannica entry has him entering parliament in 1826 as Viscount Howick, for Winchelsea. When the Whigs took power in 1830 he became under-secretary for the colonies.

There he formed his lifelong grasp of colonial questions, then as one of the advanced reformers near Wakefield. He resigned in 1834 because slave emancipation was made gradual, not immediate. As secretary at war from 1835 he reformed abuses hurting the troops in India. He resigned again in 1839, and the entry admits the pattern earned him a name for crotchetiness. His free-trade stands embarrassed his old colleagues further. The long article follows his later colonial secretaryship and his decades of colonial writing.
britannica-1911-haidinger-wilhelm-karl:
Wilhelm Karl Haidinger, an Austrian student of minerals, earth, and physics, was born at Vienna in seventeen ninety five. His father Karl had done much for the science of minerals in his day. Wilhelm went to a normal school and to classes at the university. At seventeen he joined Professor Mohs at Gratz as a pupil. Five years later he followed Mohs to the mining academy at Freiberg.

In eighteen twenty two Haidinger travelled in France and England with a count. He settled for a time in Edinburgh, in the north of Britain. There he put Mohs's work on minerals into English, with additions of his own. That work came out in three volumes in eighteen twenty five. In eighteen forty he took charge of the imperial store of minerals at Vienna. He set that store in order and made it the first in Europe.
britannica-1911-howe-richard-howe-earl:
Richard Howe, Earl Howe (1726–1799), was a British admiral, born in London on the 8th of March 1726. He was second son of Emmanuel Scrope Howe, 2nd Viscount Howe, who died governing Barbadoes in 1735. His mother was a daughter of the countess of Darlington, mistress of George I, a tie that helps explain his early rise. He entered the navy in the Severn, in Anson's squadron of 1740.

The Severn failed to round the Horn and came home. Howe next served in the Burford in the West Indies, standing in her when she was badly mauled in the failed attack on La Guayra in February 1742. He was made acting-lieutenant that year, confirmed in 1744. In the rising of 1745 he commanded the Baltimore sloop in the North Sea. The long life follows him through the Seven Years' War and the American war to the relief of Gibraltar and the Glorious First of June.
britannica-1911-huysmans-joris-karl:
Joris Karl Huysmans, a French novelist who lived from 1848 to 1907, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Paris in February 1848, he came of a family of artists of Dutch stock. He entered the ministry of the interior and was pensioned after thirty years of service. His first book, in 1874, held tales and short prose poems marked by Baudelaire.

Huysmans wrote a life of a courtesan in 1876 and a war tale for Zola's collection. A run of novels of everyday life followed, in which he outdid Zola in close realism. His novel À Rebours, in 1884, caused a sensation. It tells of the morbid tastes of a decadent aristocrat, des Esseintes. In a later book his most characteristic hero, Durtal, appears.
britannica-1911-krumbacher-carl:
Carl Krumbacher (1856–1909) was a German scholar of Byzantium, born at Kürnach in Bavaria on the 23rd of September 1856. He studied at Munich and Leipzig, and held the chair of medieval and modern Greek language and literature at Munich from 1897 until his death. His greatest work is his history of Byzantine literature, from Justinian to the fall of the Eastern Empire in 1453. A second edition came out in 1897, with help from Ehrhard on theology and Gelzer on general history, and full lists of writings throughout.

Krumbacher also founded the Byzantinische Zeitschrift in 1892 and the Byzantinisches Archiv in 1898. He travelled widely, and a journey to Greece produced his Griechische Reise (1886). Among his other works are studies of the 9th-century poetess Casia and of Michael Glykas. In 1902 he wrote strongly against the purists who wished to force the classical style back into modern Greek writing.
britannica-1911-lehrs-karl:
Karl Lehrs (1802-1878) was a German scholar of ancient Greek, and his work is surveyed in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Koenigsberg, he became professor of Greek language study there in 1845 and held the post until his death. His views were firm and strongly held.

The entry lists his main books, led by a study of Aristarchus and Homer that laid a new base for reading Homer from the text itself. His best known work was a set of popular essays on the ancient world. It also notes his stand for the single authorship of the Iliad, and his scorn for reading myths as mere symbols.
britannica-1911-ligonier-john-ligonier-e:
John Ligonier, earl Ligonier (1680-1770), rose to field marshal in British service. His Huguenot kin left Castres in south France for England late in the 1600s. He joined Marlborough's army as a volunteer. From 1702 to 1710 he fought at nearly every great siege and battle. At Malplaquet twenty-three bullets pierced his clothes and left him whole.

Long regimental rule followed: twenty-nine years with the Black Horse. Brigadier in 1735 and major-general in 1739, he rode with Lord Stair on the Rhine. George II made him a knight at Dettingen, on the field itself. At Fontenoy he led the British foot. In the Forty-Five he led the home army. At Val in 1747 his horse was killed and he was taken, then swapped within days. High posts filled his last years.
britannica-1911-macartney-george-macartn:
George Macartney, Earl Macartney, lived from 1737 to 1806. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces him to a Scots family settled in Ireland. He was born at Lissanoure in Antrim in May 1737. Trinity College, Dublin, gave him his degree in 1759. Lord Holland's circle took him up in London. In 1764 he went as envoy to Russia. There he won a treaty of alliance for England.

Seats in both parliaments followed, and a post as chief secretary for Ireland. He then governed the Caribbee Islands, and from 1780 Madras. He turned down the top post in India and came home in 1786. Made an earl in 1792, he was sent as Britain's first envoy to China. That famed mission is the act his name still carries. Ill health forced him out in 1798, and he died at Chiswick in 1806.
britannica-1911-mack-von-leiberich-karl:
Karl Mack von Leiberich (1752-1828) was an Austrian soldier born at Nenslingen in Bavaria on 25 August 1752. In 1770 he joined an Austrian cavalry regiment in which his uncle was a squadron chief. Seven years later he became an officer. In the short war of the Bavarian Succession he was picked for staff work under Count Kinsky. He did fine work there and under Field Marshal Lacy.

Mack rose to first lieutenant in 1778 and to captain on the staff in 1783. Lacy, then the first soldier of the Austrian army, held the highest view of his young aide. In 1785 Mack wed Katherine Gabrieul and was raised to noble rank as Mack von Leiberich. In the Turkish war he served on the headquarter staff. In 1789 he became lieutenant-colonel.
britannica-1911-marl:
Marl is a chalk rich clay, a mix of lime stone dust with clay like stuff. No strict sense can be set for the term, since it is used for a wide range of rocks and soils. The lime share runs from a fourth to three fourths in true marls. Past that range the stuff shades to clay or to clay rich lime rock.

Farm use made the term loose, since all sorts of earth were spread on fields in its name. True marls are soft and pale, grey or brown. They break up in water and fizz in weak sour baths. Shells, plant bits, and rare gems can hide in them.
britannica-1911-marr-carl:
Carl Marr was born in 1858 and is an American artist of note. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Milwaukee in Wisconsin, his birth city. He was born there in February 1858, the son of an engraver. He learned art from Henry Vianden in Milwaukee in his youth. He then studied at Weimar, at Berlin, and at Munich in turn.

His first work, Ahasuerus the Wandering Jew, won a medal at Munich. A canvas called Episode of 1813 hangs in the Hanover Gallery now. Germany in 1806 took a gold medal at Munich for its craft. The Flagellants, a large canvas, won gold at Munich in 1889. In 1893 he became a professor in the Munich Academy of art.
britannica-1911-mathy-karl:
Karl Mathy, who lived from 1807 to 1868, was a statesman of Baden. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his work for German unity. He was born at Mannheim in March 1807. He studied law and politics at Heidelberg and joined state finance work in 1829.

Mathy lost his post in 1834 for backing change in his paper. He lived in Swiss exile, then came back to edit papers and sit in the estates. He helped found a paper that pushed the cause of a united Germany. He sat in the Frankfurt assembly during the unrest of 1848. Later he worked in banking, then led Baden trade policy. He died at Karlsruhe in 1868, before unity came.
britannica-1911-nottingham-charles-howar:
Charles Howard, first earl of Nottingham, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in fifteen thirty six, he was the eldest son of William, first Baron Howard of Effingham. His father had served as lord high admiral. Through his father's sister the family was closely tied to Queen Elizabeth.

In Mary's reign he is said to have served at sea with his father. On Elizabeth's accession his kinship, looks, and skill secured his early rise. In fifteen fifty nine he was sent as ambassador abroad. The entry follows the career that made him lord high admiral in his own right.
britannica-1911-paarl:
Paarl, a town of the Cape Province in South Africa, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands 36 miles east-north-east of Cape Town by rail, on the west bank of the Berg river. Its people numbered 11,293 in 1904. West of it the Paarl Berg rises, crowned by three great granite boulders.

The town is set amid gardens, orange groves, and vineyards. Its two Dutch Reformed churches include an old one of colonial Dutch style, with gables, curves, and a thatched roof. Paarl is a thriving farming and wine-making centre. Its work includes wine and brandy making, wagon and carriage building, and harness making. Granite quarries lie south-east of the town. The local wines rank among South Africa's best, second only to Constantia. Paarl dates from 1687, one of the oldest European towns in the country.
britannica-1911-peters-karl:
Karl Peters, a German traveller in Africa born in 1856, was one of the founders of German East Africa, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica profiles him. Born at Neuhaus on the Elbe, the son of a Lutheran clergyman, he studied at Göttingen, Tübingen and Berlin. A gold medal from Berlin University came to him in 1879.

After a visit to London to study English principles of colonization, Peters went back to Berlin and promoted the German Colonization Society. In the autumn of 1884 he sailed with two companions to East Africa. There he concluded treaties, in his society's name, with the chiefs of Useguha, Nguru, Usagara and Ukami. Early in 1885 he formed the German East Africa Company, which soon won an imperial charter. In 1888 he undertook an expedition said to be for the relief of Emin Pasha, a move the German government had not sanctioned.
britannica-1911-rivers-anthony-woodville:
Anthony Woodville, second Earl Rivers, was a statesman and patron of letters. He lived from about fourteen forty two to fourteen eighty three. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Richard de Wydeville and Jacquetta of Luxemburg.

Rivers fought at Towton in fourteen sixty one as a young knight. He wed the daughter of Lord Scales and became a peer in fourteen sixty two. In fourteen sixty seven he faced the Bastard of Burgundy in a famed tourney. His father and brother were beheaded after Edgecot battle in fourteen sixty nine. He then took the earldom and fled with Edward to the Continent.
britannica-1911-rivers-richard-savage-4t:
Richard Savage, 4th Earl Rivers (about 1660-1712), was the second son of Thomas, 3rd Earl Rivers. When his elder brother died about 1680, he took the style of Viscount Colchester. He held that style until he came into the peerage. Young Rivers won fame as a daredevil and a rake. He was one of the most noted wild men of high society in his day.

Colchester sat in parliament for Wigan from 1681 and took a post in the Horse Guards in 1686. He was among the first men of rank to join the prince of Orange when he landed in England. He rose through army ranks with good service in Ireland and the Netherlands. He became major-general in 1693 and lieutenant-general in 1702. In 1694 he followed his father as earl.
britannica-1911-roberts-frederick-sleigh:
Frederick Sleigh Roberts, Earl Roberts, a British soldier born in 1832, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Cawnpore in India, second son of General Sir Abraham Roberts. He was educated at Eton, Sandhurst, and Addiscombe. In December 1851 he gained a commission in the Bengal Artillery.

Roberts was posted to a field battery at Peshawar, serving also as aide to his father. In 1856 he joined the quartermaster-general's department, where he stayed twenty-two years. When the Mutiny broke out in 1857, he served first with a column in the Punjab. He then joined the Delhi Field Force and was wounded in July fighting. Recovered by September, he commanded half a siege battery before Delhi. He took part in the storm of the city and its seven days of street fighting. The long life then follows his march to fame in later wars.
britannica-1911-russell-john-russell-1st:
John Russell, first Earl Russell, was a British statesman of the nineteenth century. He lived from seventeen ninety two to eighteen seventy eight. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London, the third son of the sixth duke of Bedford.

Weak health cut short Russell time at Westminster School in his youth. A private tutor taught him near Sandwich from eighteen o five to eighteen o eight. He studied at Edinburgh from eighteen o nine to eighteen twelve. In eighteen thirteen he was elected for Tavistock and entered parliament young. He fought moves to join Norway and Sweden in foreign policy debates. At home he opposed harsh laws and pushed for reform of ills.
britannica-1911-spencer-john-charles-spe:
John Charles Spencer, third Earl Spencer, was an English statesman of note. He lived from seventeen eighty two to eighteen forty five. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Men knew him best as Lord Althorp during his father life time.

Spencer was born at Spencer House, London, in May seventeen eighty two. His father, the second earl, built the finest private library in Europe. In eighteen hundred the son entered Trinity College, Cambridge, to study there. He worked hard at mathematics, yet spent most time hunting and racing. After his degree in eighteen o two he toured the Continent at length. War cut that tour short, and he entered parliament in eighteen o four.
britannica-1911-spencer-john-poyntz-spen:
John Poyntz Spencer, fifth Earl Spencer, was an English statesman born in eighteen thirty five. He was the son of the fourth earl and a daughter of William Poyntz of Cowdray. Schooled at Harrow and at Trinity College, Cambridge, he sat briefly in parliament. He succeeded to the earldom in December eighteen fifty seven, at a young age. His long career as a Liberal dates from eighteen sixty eight.

In that year Spencer became lord lieutenant of Ireland under Gladstone. He held that post until eighteen seventy four in his first term. When the Liberals returned in eighteen eighty he became lord president of the council. In eighteen eighty two he began a second term as lord lieutenant of Ireland. Those three years were a time of great disorder and plots in Ireland. His courage and firmness then won the praise of all sides.
britannica-1911-weizsacker-karl:
Karl Weizsaecker (1822-1899) was a German Protestant theologian, and his work is set out in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Oehringen in Wuerttemberg, he studied at Tuebingen and Berlin. He began teaching at Tuebingen in 1847 and became professor of church and dogmatic history there in 1861.

The entry says his wide fame rests on two large studies, one on the gospel history, its sources, and its growth, and one on the apostolic age of the Christian church. The second ran to a fresh edition and an English version in the 1890s. He also helped edit a theology journal for more than twenty years, and died in August 1899.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-xavie:
Francis Xavier Haberl, born at Oberellenbach in Lower Bavaria on 12 April 1840 and dead at Ratisbon on 5 September 1910. He was a historian of sacred music and founder of a school that reformed church singing across the Catholic world. Ordained at Passau in 1862, he showed a decided gift for music and directed seminary music. From 1867 to 1870 he served as choirmaster at Santa Maria dell'Anima in Rome while pursuing historical research. From 1871 to 1882 he directed the Ratisbon cathedral choir in one of its most brilliant periods.

In 1874 he founded a church-music school at Ratisbon with three professors and three pupils. It grew into the centre where priests and laymen from every country learned to carry out reform in their dioceses. His foresight gave the school an endowment and built beside it the church of St. Cecilia, where pupils practised what they learned in theory.
daddy-s-girl:
A tale for girls by L. T. Meade fills Daddy's Girl, issued by the A. L. Burt Company of New York. Meade lists her other girls' books on the title page, among them A Very Naughty Girl and Polly. The record dates this edition 1908, and the book runs to twenty-three chapters.

Philip Ogilvie and his wife quarrel in their Belgrave Square drawing room as the tale opens. Their daughter, eight years old and called the Angel, dresses happily upstairs, unaware. Talk of a lovely place named Silverbel, and of a ship that will bring wealth when it comes in, fills the middle. Meade builds a home story on a child's love set against her parents' strife.
doe-osti-3363382-solar-radiation-researc:
Manajit Sengupta, Aron Habte, Yu Xie, and colleagues report on fiscal years 2022 through 2024 at the Solar Radiation Research Laboratory. The report is NLR/TP-5D00-98206, dated May 2026. The National Laboratory of the Rockies runs the lab. It is a leading site for solar measurement and sensor calibration. It also keeps the World Radiation Reference for the United States. That reference is the standard behind solar readings nationwide.

The report covers applied solar radiation measurement, calibration, and standards work. The team helped revise the ISO guide on pyranometer use. The new guide speaks to modern digital sensors with built-in checks. The team also tested modeled ultraviolet output against ground readings at the Golden, Colorado station. Across sites, the mean error stayed within 8 percent.
eastern-shame-girl:
George Soulié de Morant translated a set of Chinese love tales in Eastern Shame Girl, privately printed at New York in 1929. A note at the front says the stories come from the classic literature of China in the seventeenth century. The title tale opens in the Wan-li period. A young student named Li comes to Peking for the examinations. He falls in with the city's pleasure seekers.

Six more tales follow. They tell of a wedding, a strange destiny, and an embroidered slipper's error. A counterfeit old woman, a monastery, and a complicated marriage round out the set. Love in these stories meets law, ghosts, and cruel fate. One faithless man is sentenced to slow death, while his lover's friend burns incense for her soul at every feast. A later edition, as Chinese Love Tales in 1935, was attacked in court and acquitted, a note records.
ethel-hollister-s-second-summer-as-a-cam:
Irene Elliott Benson published Ethel Hollister's Second Summer as a Campfire Girl in 1912, and the book opens with a summary of the earlier volume. There, Ethel became a Camp Fire Girl through her great-aunt Susan Carpenter of Akron, Ohio, a wealthy woman known for her gifts to charity.

Contents and scenes trace a busy season: firm friendship with Harvey, a second trip, life at camp again, a visit from Mrs. Hollister, and the arrival of the Scouts. One girl gives service, another proves a heroine on a woodland path, and Mattie makes good. The season closes with camp breaking up, a wedding for Judge Sands and Kate, and surprises at Christmas. Readers get a cheerful girls' story about camp craft, loyalty, and growing up.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CroftRobertEarl: An FBI memorandum sent to the Special Agent in Charge in Denver deals with other evidence concerning Lee Harvey Oswald, the accused killer of President Kennedy. The memo is filed under the name Robert Earl Croft. Beyond its routing and subject line, the surviving record gives no detail about which evidence the Denver office was being sent or why it mattered.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RayJamesEarlCA7:
Harold Weisberg filed this complaint in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia. He sued the Department of Justice and the Department of State under the Freedom of Information Act. The records he sought concerned the extradition of James Earl Ray from foreign countries. Ray had fled abroad after the King assassination and was captured in London.

Extradition paper crosses two governments, which gave Weisberg two defendants. His complaint asks the court to order the records produced. Suits like this were his life's second half: the King case fought as paperwork. The complaint preserves his legal theory, the agencies he named, and the episode, Ray's flight and return, that the records would document.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TurnerCarlCMajo: Morton Mintz reported in the Washington Post that Senate investigators accused four sergeants of splitting $100,000 in thirteen months. The article, filed under Major General Carl Turner's name, covers charges of military corruption. Investigators said the money came from crooked dealings around army clubs and supplies. Mintz, a noted investigative reporter, lays out what the probers claimed and what the figures showed.
happy-pollyooly-the-rich-little-poor-gir:
Edgar Jepson published Happy Pollyooly, the sequel to his Pollyooly, in 1915, with pictures by Reginald Birch. Pollyooly is a London child of the slums who earns her living by her wits, playing parts and running errands for the great. The contents open with the Honourable John Ruffin making an arrangement, and Hilary Vance finding a confidante. Infuriated swains and a duchess with an idea follow. Pollyooly is called in, and plays her favorite part.

Her favorite part is herself in disguise, a boy or a page as the job requires. She plays the good Samaritan too, and settles the affairs of her betters with Cockney sense. Jepson writes with pace and affection for his small heroine. The subtitle calls her the rich little poor girl: rich in nerve, loyalty, and luck. The book is a bright specimen of Edwardian light fiction.
jill-a-flower-girl:
Jill: A Flower Girl is a novel by L. T. Meade, published in 1892. It opens on a warm night in London at the height of the season. Outside a great Grosvenor Square mansion, a crowd of poor onlookers watches rich guests arrive for a reception. The fine dresses and carriages turn the street into a free fairy spectacle for them.

At the front of the crowd stands Jill, a girl of about sixteen. She is tall, neat, and clean, with a colored scarf wound like a turban round her head. On her arm she carries a flat basket of roses, narcissus, and forget-me-nots to sell. Two younger boys stand with her. From this sharp gap between street and mansion, Meade builds her flower girl's story.
light-o-the-morning-the-story-of-an-iris:
L. T. Meade tells the story of Nora, an Irish girl. Chapter Two warns that some more of the land must go. The Wild Murphys and the Squire's trouble darken her home life. An invitation and a diamond cross promise change.

Contents promise a cave of the banshee and Molly's appearance. Nora faces shame, slang, and two revealing letters. A compact and a cheeky Irish girl chapter add complications. Meade aims the tale at young readers fond of Ireland. Education and other things occupy chapter nine of Nora's story. Two descriptions and a compact deepen the household tensions later.
phebe-the-blackberry-girl: Hosted here, the sample shows only the front matter of Phebe, the Blackberry Girl, the title pages, a short series introduction, and contents, with no story text visible. The book belongs to Uncle Thomas's Stories for Good Children, printed at Worcester by Edward Livermore in 1850. The introduction says the series aims to give the young information joined with amusement, and hopes the stories will breed a love of good books. The one tale here is told in two parts.
poems-by-a-little-girl:
Hilda Conkling wrote the poems in this book while she was still a small child. The poet Amy Lowell supplied a preface arguing that they are real poetry, not a curiosity. Lowell marvels at the rare case of an author whose childhood and career arrive at the same time. Many pieces had already appeared in magazines such as Poetry, St. Nicholas, and Good Housekeeping before the book gathered them.

The opening poem, dedicated to her mother, promises a song and a poem twisted into one, with a curl of cloud and a feather of blue. Conkling's subjects are dreams, secrets, sky, and the wish to make her mother happy, handled with an ear Lowell insists adults should take seriously. The book remains a famous test case in how young a true poet can be.
polly-a-new-fashioned-girl:
L. T. Meade wrote Polly, a New-Fashioned Girl, published in New York in 1910. Meade, author of A World of Girls and dozens of other school stories, specialized in heroines who run things, and her Polly is new-fashioned indeed. Early chapters announce a great misfortune, introduce the family, and urge the heroine to be brave. Then Polly hatches quite a new sort of scheme and launches a raid that alarms the grown-ups.

Contents promise the classic Meade machinery. Strangers may or may not be allowed to come. Limits are tested, an indigestion week is played for comedy, and lessons come without a sermon on every page. Polly's energy, practicality, and refusal to mope made her a favorite, and the book shows girls' fiction changing with its readers.
sara-a-princess-the-story-of-a-noble-gir: Fannie E. Newberry wrote Sara, A Princess, the story of a noble girl, under a short verse that calls Sara a princess not by birth. Her title, the verse says, is from above, her heritage the right of worth, and her empire that of love. The contents list chapters opening with Omens, Good and Ill, Storm and Trouble, and A Search and Its Ending.
somebody-s-little-girl:
Martha Young gives her tale Somebody's Little Girl to two little Elizabeths: Elizabeth Young and Elizabeth Magruder. The tale turns on what Bessie Bell recalls. If the teller just told the things Bessie Bell recalls, she warns, they would sound very strange. Bessie Bell does not know whether she recalls them, just knows them, or whether they grew in some strange country that never was in the world.

Wise grown folk tell her no such things exist. Yet she recalls a window from which one could look out and see all green, little and green, and always shifting and moving, away beyond all. She recalls, too, little apple trees all alike, in rows stacked row on row, up to a great row of big round red apples on top of all. A small round red apple once made her heart jump and thump at the memory.
sparrows-the-story-of-an-unprotected-gir: Horace W. C. Newte wrote Sparrows. The sub-title calls it The Story of an Unprotected Girl. The contents run to thirty-six numbered chapters. Each chapter bears a name for its turn. One is The Devitts and Two is Mavis Keeves. Three is Friends in Need. Later heads name Mavis Leaves Her Nest. Barren Ways and Spider and Fly follow. Mavis's Prayer, Surrender, and Springtime stand in the run. The Way of All Flesh comes at Twenty. Snares, Travail, and a nursing home mark the later tale.
star-dust-a-story-of-an-american-girl:
Fannie Hurst tells the tale of Lilly Becker in Star-Dust. Its sub-title calls it A Story of an American Girl. The book is dated 1921. Book One bears the head The Vine. In Chapter I, Lilly picks out a piano piece with one hand. Rubinstein's Melody in F is that stubborn piece. Her young mind drifts as she plays into a bright realm.

Spring shows lacy in her daydream through song. Fountains toss up bubbles of pure aria there. A Greek row of youth stands posed toward her. School folk make up that row. Estelle Foote is her winning rival in it. Sydney Prothero shows his sure spitball aim. Miss Lare wears her glasses low on her nose. Then her mother calls down through the floor register. That call always comes in the practice hour after school.
the-black-pearl:
Mrs Wilson Woodrow published a desert novel with Appleton in New York and London in August 1912. Woodrow is also named for Sally Salt and The New Missioner. An illustration list includes a frontispiece captioned with a character feeling particularly good.

Chapter one begins at sunset as a train that has crawled across a desert stops at the village of Paloma, not many miles from the Salton Sea. After a delay, one lone passenger gets down. Other picture captions promise a woman called the Black Pearl standing alone. One shows a girl bending over a man while holding a branch. Both hint at a central female figure in a harsh place.
the-case-and-the-girl: The Case and the Girl, by Randall Parrish, dated 1922, opens with its table of contents. Twenty chapters are headed. They run from The Lady in the Limousine and A Sudden Engagement through the Coolidge home. Miss Coolidge Explains and West Wins the First Hand follow. A visit to the indigent and a new Miss Coolidge come next. Then come the body of a suicide, suspicion verified, and 238 Wray Street. West Makes His Choice, Facing Death, and What the Telephone Told close the list. No page of the story is shown.
the-chinese-boy-and-girl:
Isaac Taylor Headland of Peking University, author of Chinese Mother Goose Rhymes, wrote this study of Chinese child life. His preface admits the limits of his view at the start. No full study, he says, can be made until Chinese homes open freely to Western eyes.

Glimpses, though, are plentiful enough to give a fair idea of that life. The playground is rarely hidden, least of all in the street, and Chinese nurses bring rhymes, stories, and games into foreign homes. He praises Chinese kindergarten methods for their ingenuity and their power to hold and teach children. Traveling shows and jugglers, he adds, are plentiful and aimed chiefly at the young. His large collection of toys shows many matches with toys common in other lands, and he concludes that the Chinese child shares much with children everywhere.
the-daughter-of-the-chieftain-the-story-:
Edward S. Ellis subtitles The Daughter of the Chieftain the story of an Indian girl. Chapter One, headed Omas, Alice, and Linna, first explains the game of jack stones. Toss a ball, and catch up iron prongs one at a time while it is aloft, then two, three, and four at once. Older players, the narrator says, once made do with pieces of stone.

The tale then settles on Alice Ripley, a little girl playing the game near her log home on the first of July, 1778. Her house has no carpets or stove, only a big fireplace where food is made ready. The place is the famed Wyoming Valley in western Pennsylvania, between the Blue Ridge and the Alleghany Mountains, with the beautiful Susquehanna River running through it for twenty-one miles.
the-diary-of-a-goose-girl:
Kate Douglas Wiggin's The Diary of a Goose Girl came out in London from Gay and Bird in 1902, with illustrations by Claude A. Shepperson. Wiggin inscribes the book to the hens, ducks, and geese who so kindly gave her sittings for the sketches. Chapter I is headed Thornycroft Farm, near Barbury Green, July 1, 190-.

Calling herself a goose girl, she says, is using only the most modest of her titles: she is also a poultry-maid, a tender of Belgian hares and rabbits, and a shepherdess. She fancies the goose-girl role because it recalls the German fairy tales of her youth, when she yearned to be just what she now is. Jolting along charming Sussex roads behind a fat buff pony in a tippy cart, she came upon the village of Barbury Green.
the-goose-girl: Harold MacGrath wrote The Goose Girl. The Bobbs-Merrill Company printed it in Indianapolis in 1909. Pictures are by Andre Castaigne. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of twenty-three chapters. The heads run from Some in Rags and An American Consul. They run through For Her Country, The Young Vintner, and At the Black Eagle. They name The King's Letter, Twin Lockets, and Happiness. A picture caption says they acclaimed her the queen. No chapter text is present.
the-jungle-girl:
Gordon Casserly published this Indian romance in New York in 1922. He had written The Elephant God before it. Chapter I is called The Grey Boar. It opens with a pigsticking song. Daring courage, a firm seat, and an eagle eye are its demands. Mrs. Norton then studies herself in a long mirror. She wears a well-cut grey habit and long boots. Wavy auburn hair frames a pretty face under her sun-helmet.

She picks up her whip next. She passes her sleeping husband's door quietly. She descends the Residency's broad marble staircase. A servant in a long red coat hurries to open the door. The contents promise the world she rides into. Youth calls to youth there. A crocodile intervenes, and exile is sentenced. A border outpost and a forest girl wait in the Terai. Tiger land, devil dancers, and a strange rescue follow.
the-lilac-girl:
Ralph Henry Barbour published his novel in 1909 with color pictures by Clarence F. Underwood. Chapter one finds two men beside a campfire at Saddle Pass, a notch in the Sangre de Cristo Range in southern Colorado. June summer fills the valleys below while mountain evenings stay chill.

Firelight warms tired bodies as daylight lingers over the pass. Barbour wrote many books for young readers, and the picture captions here promise a girl glancing over lilac sprays at a man named Wade. Ranch country, mining money, and a courtship tested by pride shape the story ahead.
the-poor-little-rich-girl:
Eleanor Gates's The Poor Little Rich Girl, published by Grosset and Dunlap at New York, opens with a small crisis in a nursery. Halfway up the gilt-framed pier glass stands a tiny ink line that Gwendolyn drew the evening before, when she was six. Now it is the morning of her seventh birthday. She straightens herself to her utmost height against the mirror a second time.

Her yellow head does not reach the mark by the smallest part of an inch. The worst is true: she has not grown a whit taller in the night. Her face whitens, her eyes swim, and she crosses the nursery in tears to fling herself among the pillows of the window seat. An illustration caption notes how rare it is for Gwendolyn to have father and mother in the nursery together. That hints at the absence that frames her troubles.
the-red-cross-girl:
Richard Harding Davis's stories are introduced by Gouverneur Morris, who recalls Davis as almost too good to be true and as a man the gods loved, so that he died young. Morris describes playing at pirates and sperm whales with him within the year and ransacking the Westchester Hills for gun sites against a feared Mexican invasion.

Nine stories follow the introduction, headed by the title piece and including a grand cross of the crescent, an invasion of England, a sailorman, a mind reader, and a card-sharp. The introduction's affectionate portrait sets the tone. Readers meet Davis first as a beloved friend, then as a writer of brisk adventure tales.
the-story-girl: L. M. Montgomery, author of Anne of Green Gables, dedicated this children's novel to her cousin Frederica E. Campbell in remembrance of old days, old dreams, and old laughter. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The contents list chapters such as The Home of Our Fathers. Legends of the Old Orchard and Peter Goes to Church follow. The Blue Chest of Rachel Ward and Forbidden Fruit come next. The Story Girl's tales themselves do not appear.
the-stowaway-girl: Louis Tracy, author of The Wings of the Morning, published this adventure novel with Grosset and Dunlap, under Edward J. Clode's copyrights of 1909 and 1912, illustrated by Nesbit Benson. Only the title pages and contents appear in this record. The contents list fifteen chapters. They follow the Andromeda out and home. Her refugees and cross purposes on the high seas come next. A lively morning in Exchange Buildings follows. The lure of gold appears too. Brazil choosing her president closes the list. The stowaway's story itself does not appear.
winnie-childs-the-shop-girl: Nothing but the title page and contents is present here for C. N. and A. M. Williamson's Winnie Childs, the Shop Girl, printed in 1914 and 1916, so the story does not appear. The contents open with a chapter called The Dryad Door. Balm of Gilead and an ill wind follow. Later chapters name the kindness of Miss Rolls, scenes for a movie, and hands with rings. Two Peters enter the list. A test of character and Peter Rolls's little ways close the part shown.
